blocks.v: ES6 (2015) and later versions introduced syntax that makes JavaScript shorter, safer, and easier to reason about. You will see these patterns in almost every modern codebase, so treat them as the default way to write JS, not an optional extra.
Pull values out of arrays/objects in one line, and copy or merge them without mutating the original.

Arrow functions inherit `this` from their surrounding scope instead of rebinding it — this is why they are preferred for callbacks. Template literals let you interpolate expressions directly into strings.
`document.querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` accept any CSS selector, so you rarely need the older `getElementById`/`getElementsByClassName` APIs.

const card = document.querySelector('.card');
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('button.primary');
Prefer `textContent` over `innerHTML` when inserting plain text — it is faster and avoids accidental HTML/script injection.
Build elements in memory before attaching them to the page — this avoids multiple expensive reflows.
Wrap code that can fail in `try`, handle the failure in `catch`, and use `finally` for cleanup that must run either way.
Throw an `Error` (or a subclass of it) rather than a plain string — it carries a stack trace and a consistent `.message` shape.
`try/catch` works with `await` directly — no `.catch()` chaining needed.
A React component is just a function that returns JSX. Props are the read-only arguments passed in from the parent.

Never mutate a prop inside the component that receives it — treat it the same way you would treat a function argument in any pure function. If the UI needs to change, that change should come from the parent re-rendering with new props, or from local state.
Break UI into small components and compose them via `children` or nested JSX — this keeps each piece focused and reusable.

Calling the state setter schedules a re-render with the new value — it does not mutate the variable in place. When the next state depends on the previous one, pass a function to avoid stale-closure bugs.
The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs. An empty array means "run once on mount." Always return a cleanup function for subscriptions, timers, or listeners.
Both hooks skip recomputing a value/function unless their dependencies change — use them for expensive calculations or to keep a stable reference passed into a memoized child component.

A custom hook is just a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks internally. It lets you extract and reuse stateful logic across components without changing your component tree.
The consuming component uses it exactly like `useState` — the persistence logic is completely hidden.
Git tracks files through three states: **working directory** (your edits), **staging area** (changes marked for the next commit), and the **repository** (committed history).

git status          # see what changed and where
git add file.js      # working directory → staging area
git commit -m "msg"  # staging area → repository
Every commit has a hash, author, and message — this is what lets you inspect, diff, and revert to any past state.

git log --oneline --graph
git show <commit-hash>
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit — creating one is instant and cheap, so branch freely for any change of scope.

git branch feature/login       # create
git switch feature/login       # switch
git switch -c feature/signup   # create + switch in one step
A **fast-forward** merge just moves the branch pointer forward when there is no divergent history. A **three-way merge** creates a new commit that joins two diverged histories.

git switch main
git merge feature/login

# if conflicts appear, Git marks them inline:
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# your change
# =======
# their change
# >>>>>>> feature/login
Once a branch is merged, it has served its purpose — delete it to keep the branch list meaningful.

git branch -d feature/login   # safe delete — refuses if not merged
git branch -D feature/login   # force delete

Rebasing replays your commits on top of another branch's latest state instead of creating a merge commit — the result is a linear history, at the cost of rewriting commit hashes. Never rebase commits that have already been pushed and shared with others.

git switch feature/login
git rebase main
Interactive rebase lets you edit, reorder, squash, or drop commits before they are shared — useful for cleaning up a messy branch into a small number of meaningful commits.

git rebase -i HEAD~4

# opens an editor:
pick a1b2c3d Add login form
squash e4f5g6h Fix typo
squash h7i8j9k Fix another typo
pick k1l2m3n Add validation
`git reflog` records every position `HEAD` has been at — it is your safety net if a rebase goes wrong.

git reflog
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}   # restore to the state before the rebase

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed systems, introduced by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. It defines a set of constraints that, when followed, produce scalable, cacheable, stateless web services. REST is not a protocol or standard — it's a design philosophy built on top of HTTP.

**The Six REST Constraints**
1. **Client-Server** — UI and data storage are separated
2. **Stateless** — every request contains all information needed; no session on server
3. **Cacheable** — responses must define whether they can be cached
4. **Uniform Interface** — consistent resource identification and manipulation
5. **Layered System** — client doesn't know if it talks to the actual server or a proxy
6. **Code on Demand** (optional) — server can send executable code (e.g., JavaScript)
A resource is any named entity your API exposes — a user, an order, a product. URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers) identify resources. Good URI design is predictable and expressive.
**Resources are nouns, HTTP methods are verbs.** The method + URI together describe an action: `DELETE /users/42` is clear. `POST /deleteUser` is not RESTful.

Statelessness means each HTTP request must contain all information the server needs to fulfill it. The server holds no session state between requests. This makes REST APIs horizontally scalable — any server instance can handle any request.
**JWT is the stateless auth pattern.** The token carries the user identity and is verified cryptographically — no database lookup needed on every request.
A well-designed REST API is predictable, consistent, and easy to integrate. These conventions are widely adopted and should be your defaults.

URIs identify **things** (resources), HTTP methods describe **actions**.
Use plural nouns: `/users`, `/products`, `/orders`.
Never put verbs in URIs — the HTTP method is the verb.
Every request must be self-contained — don't rely on server session state.
Always paginate list endpoints — never return unbounded arrays.
Use consistent error response shapes so API consumers can handle errors uniformly.
Version your API: `/v1/users` or via Accept header: `Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json`.

sections.title: HTTP as the Language of the Web

blocks.v: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the protocol REST APIs are built on. Every API call is an HTTP request with a method, a URI, headers, and optionally a body — and every response has a status code, headers, and optionally a body.

**Key Properties of HTTP Methods**
• **Safe** — does not change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS)
• **Idempotent** — calling it multiple times has the same effect as calling it once (GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD)
• **Non-idempotent** — multiple calls create multiple effects (POST)
These properties matter for reliability: if a GET request fails mid-flight, you can safely retry it. If a POST fails, you must be careful not to accidentally create duplicate resources.
GET retrieves data. POST submits data to be processed — typically to create a new resource. These are the two most commonly used methods.
PUT replaces a resource entirely. PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes a resource. All three are idempotent — calling them multiple times produces the same result.
**PUT vs PATCH:** Use PUT when replacing a full resource and you can send all its fields. Use PATCH for partial updates — it's more efficient and less risky (no accidental null-ing of fields).
HTTP status codes are 3-digit numbers that communicate the outcome of a request. They're grouped into five classes by the first digit.

**The Five Classes**
• **1xx — Informational** — request received, continuing (rarely seen)
• **2xx — Success** — request was received, understood, and accepted
• **3xx — Redirection** — further action needed (follow the Location header)
• **4xx — Client Error** — the request was wrong (bad input, unauthorized, not found)
• **5xx — Server Error** — the server failed to fulfill a valid request
The rule of thumb: if it starts with 4, the caller made a mistake and should fix their request. If it starts with 5, something broke on the server side.

sections.title: Common Status Codes and Things to Remember

blocks.v:
200 OK             // Success — generic, used with GET/PUT/PATCH
201 Created        // New resource created — use after POST
204 No Content     // Success but no body — use after DELETE

301 Moved Permanently  // Old URL redirected forever
304 Not Modified       // Cached response is still valid

400 Bad Request    // Malformed request syntax or invalid input
401 Unauthorized   // Missing or invalid authentication
403 Forbidden      // Authenticated but not allowed
404 Not Found      // Resource doesn't exist
409 Conflict       // Resource conflict (e.g., duplicate email)
422 Unprocessable  // Input parsed but validation failed
429 Too Many Req.  // Rate limit exceeded

500 Internal Server Error  // Generic server crash
502 Bad Gateway            // Upstream service failed
503 Service Unavailable    // Server down for maintenance

Always return the most specific status code — `422` for validation, `409` for conflicts, not just `400` for everything.
`401` means "prove who you are"; `403` means "I know who you are, but no".
Use `201` after POST (created), `204` after DELETE (no body to return).
Never return `200` with an error message in the body — use the correct 4xx/5xx code.
Log every `5xx` error server-side with a full stack trace for debugging.
These two terms are often confused but represent distinct security concerns.

**Authentication** — Who are you? Verifying the identity of the caller. (Login, token validation)
**Authorization** — What can you do? Verifying the caller has permission to access the resource. (Role checks, ownership checks)

In a typical REST API: the client authenticates once (receives a token), then presents that token on every subsequent request. The server verifies the token (authentication) and then checks whether that identity is allowed to access the specific resource (authorization).
A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe token that carries claims (key-value data) and a cryptographic signature. It consists of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots.
**JWTs are signed, not encrypted.** Anyone can decode the payload with Base64. Never put passwords, PII, or secrets in the payload — only IDs and non-sensitive claims.
The server signs the token on login using a secret key. On subsequent requests, the server verifies the signature — if it matches, the payload is trusted. No database lookup needed.

Short-lived access tokens minimise the damage if a token is stolen. A refresh token (longer-lived) lets the client get a new access token without re-entering credentials — giving users a seamless session.
**Security rule:** Store access tokens in memory (not localStorage). Store refresh tokens in `httpOnly` cookies — JavaScript cannot read them, preventing XSS attacks.

Authentication = identity; Authorization = permission. They are different steps.
JWTs are signed but **not encrypted** — never put secrets or passwords in the payload.
Keep access tokens short-lived (15m–1h); use refresh tokens for session continuity.
Store access tokens in memory; store refresh tokens in `httpOnly` cookies.
Always use HTTPS — tokens transmitted over HTTP are trivially stolen.
Rotate your JWT secret immediately if it is ever exposed.
JWT cannot be invalidated before expiry unless you maintain a blocklist (denylist) — plan accordingly.

TypeScript is JavaScript with a static type system. It compiles to plain JavaScript and adds zero runtime overhead. The payoff: the compiler catches entire categories of bugs before you run a single line of code — type mismatches, missing properties, wrong function arguments.

**What TypeScript Gives You**
• Compile-time type checking — catch bugs before runtime
• Excellent IDE support — autocompletion, refactoring, inline docs
• Self-documenting code — types describe what a function expects and returns
• Safer refactoring — the compiler tells you what broke
• Gradual adoption — add types incrementally to any JS project
TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript — every valid JS file is valid TypeScript. You adopt it incrementally.
Type annotations use a colon after the name. TypeScript also infers types from assigned values — you don't need to annotate everything.
**Avoid `any`.** It disables type checking entirely. Use `unknown` when you truly don't know the type — then narrow it before use.
TypeScript provides typed arrays, tuples (fixed-length typed arrays), and enums (named sets of constants).
Union types say a value can be one of several types. Intersection types combine multiple types into one. Both are fundamental to writing flexible, type-safe code.

Prefer inferred types — only annotate when the compiler can't figure it out.
Never use `any` — use `unknown` and narrow it before use.
Literal unions (`'GET' | 'POST'`) are safer than plain `string` for constrained values.
Use string enums for debuggability — numeric enums print as opaque numbers.
Intersection types are additive (must satisfy all); union types are alternatives (can satisfy one).
Empty array inference: annotate `const users: User[] = []` — without it TypeScript infers `never[]`.
Both interfaces and type aliases define the shape of an object. They're very similar but with key differences that matter in practice.

**Key Differences**
• **Declaration merging** — interfaces can be declared multiple times and TypeScript merges them. Type aliases cannot.
• **Extension** — interfaces use `extends`; type aliases use `&` intersection.
• **Unions** — only type aliases can express union types.
• **implements** — both work with class `implements`.
**Rule of thumb:** Use `interface` for object shapes and public APIs. Use `type` for unions, primitives, tuples, and complex mapped types.
An interface declares the shape an object must conform to. It can describe properties, methods, and call signatures.
Optional properties (`?`) may be absent. Readonly properties cannot be reassigned after initialisation. Index signatures describe objects with dynamic keys.
Interfaces can extend other interfaces to add properties. Classes use `implements` to declare they satisfy an interface — the compiler enforces it.
**Program to interfaces.** Accept interfaces as parameter types — this decouples code and makes testing easy by allowing mock implementations.

Use `interface` for object shapes and public APIs — supports declaration merging.
Use `type` for unions, tuples, primitives, and complex mapped types.
Mark truly immutable properties as `readonly` — the compiler enforces it.
Optional (`?`) means the property can be absent — always guard before accessing its value.
Interfaces are structural — an object satisfies an interface if it has the right shape, regardless of type name.
Prefer interface `extends` over type intersections for object inheritance — better error messages.

sections.title: What Are Generics and Why They Matter

blocks.v: Generics let you write reusable, type-safe code that works with different types without sacrificing type information. They're the TypeScript mechanism for parameterising types just like functions parameterise values.
A generic function declares a type parameter between angle brackets. TypeScript infers the type argument from the call-site — you rarely need to provide it explicitly.
Generics work in interfaces and classes — making data structures like stacks, queues, and repositories fully type-safe.
Constraints (`extends`) limit which types a type parameter accepts. Utility types are built-in generics for transforming existing types — used constantly in real TypeScript code.

Generics preserve type information that `any` discards — always prefer them.
TypeScript infers generic parameters — you rarely need to specify them explicitly.
Use constraints (`extends`) to limit a type parameter while keeping flexibility.
Memorise the utility types: `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `Exclude`, `Extract`.
`keyof T` gives a union of all property key names of T.

Angular is a full-featured, opinionated front-end framework maintained by Google. Unlike React (a library) or Vue (a progressive framework), Angular is a complete platform — routing, HTTP, forms, animations, and dependency injection are all built in.

**Angular's Core Building Blocks**
• **Components** — UI pieces with template, logic, and styles
• **Services** — shared business logic and data access, injected via DI
• **Modules** — feature groupings (NgModules) or standalone (Angular 14+)
• **Directives** — modify the behaviour or appearance of DOM elements
• **Pipes** — transform displayed values in templates
• **Routing** — client-side navigation between views
Angular is built with TypeScript from the ground up. Its strong conventions make it particularly well-suited for large enterprise applications.

sections.title: Setting Up with the Angular CLI

blocks.v: The Angular CLI (`@angular/cli`) handles project creation, file generation, building, testing, and serving. It's the standard entry point for every Angular project.
**Always use the CLI for file generation.** It creates components with correct naming, wires them into the module, and generates spec files automatically.
An Angular component is a TypeScript class decorated with `@Component`. The decorator configures the selector, template, and styles. The class contains the logic.
Angular has four data binding syntaxes that connect the component class to the template. Mastering all four is fundamental.
Hello, {{ username }}!
**Mnemonic:** `[]` = into the DOM, `()` = out of the DOM, `[()]` = both directions (banana in a box).

Always use `ng generate` — it handles naming, wiring, and spec file creation.
Component `selector` is how you use it in HTML: `'app-user-card'` → ``.
Data binding: `{{ }}` for display, `[]` for properties, `()` for events, `[()]` for two-way.
Angular enforces TypeScript — lean into it, don't work around it with `any`.
Components declared in a module are only available within that module (unless exported).

Angular calls lifecycle hook methods at key moments in a component's life — from creation to destruction. Implementing the right hook at the right time is essential for correct behaviour and preventing memory leaks.
**Always unsubscribe in ngOnDestroy.** Observable subscriptions that are never unsubscribed cause memory leaks. Use the `async` pipe where possible — it auto-unsubscribes.
Structural directives modify the DOM layout by adding, removing, or replacing elements. They're prefixed with `*` in templates.

Welcome, {{ user.name }}!

Please log in.
  • {{ i + 1 }}. {{ item.name }}
trackById(index: number, item: any): number { return item.id; }

Active

Pending

Unknown
**Always use trackBy with *ngFor** on lists that can change. Without it, Angular re-creates all DOM nodes on every update — a major performance issue for large lists.
Components communicate through `@Input()` (parent passes data to child) and `@Output()` (child emits events to parent via EventEmitter).

Pipes transform how values appear in templates without changing the underlying data. The `async` pipe is especially important — it subscribes to Observables and auto-unsubscribes when the component is destroyed.

{{ name | uppercase }} {{ price | currency:'USD' }} {{ date | date:'mediumDate' }} {{ text | slice:0:100 }} {{ user | json }} {{ users$ | async }}
  • {{ u.name }}
@Pipe({ name: 'truncate' }) export class TruncatePipe implements PipeTransform { transform(value: string, limit = 50): string { return value.length > limit ? value.slice(0, limit) + '…' : value; } } // Usage: {{ description | truncate:80 }}

Lifecycle order: `constructor → ngOnChanges → ngOnInit → ngAfterViewInit → ngOnDestroy`.
Fetch data in `ngOnInit` — DI is ready but inputs aren't set in the constructor.
Always unsubscribe in `ngOnDestroy` — use the `async` pipe wherever possible to auto-manage subscriptions.
Use `trackBy` with all `*ngFor` on changeable lists.
`@Input()` = data flowing in; `@Output()` + EventEmitter = events flowing out.
The `async` pipe is the preferred way to consume observables in templates.

A service is a TypeScript class decorated with `@Injectable()` that contains logic not tied to any specific component — data fetching, business rules, state management, logging. Services are the home for everything shared across multiple components.

**What Belongs in a Service**
• HTTP calls and API communication
• Authentication and user session management
• Shared state (cart, user preferences, notifications)
• Business logic (calculations, validation rules)
• Caching and data transformation
Rule: if two components need the same data or logic, it belongs in a service — not duplicated in both.
Using `providedIn: 'root'` registers the service in the root injector — a singleton available everywhere in the app without explicit module imports.

DI is a design pattern where a class receives its dependencies from the outside rather than creating them. Angular's hierarchical DI system wires everything automatically — the injector reads TypeScript constructor parameter types and resolves them.
Angular's `HttpClient` returns RxJS Observables — a powerful async primitive that supports operators for transformation, error handling, retry, and cancellation.

Use `providedIn: 'root'` for app-wide singletons. Use component `providers` for scoped instances.
Services are the single source of truth for shared data — never duplicate logic between components.
HttpClient methods return cold Observables — nothing happens until you subscribe (or use the `async` pipe).
Handle errors in service methods with `catchError` — don't let raw HTTP errors reach components.
DI makes testing easy — provide a mock service in tests without touching component code.
Use RxJS operators — `map`, `tap`, `switchMap`, `debounceTime` — to transform and control data streams.
The `async` pipe auto-subscribes and auto-unsubscribes — prefer it over manual subscription in templates.

title: Git Branching at Work: Alex & Maya's Story

blocks.v: 📍 Monday, 9:02 AM — The #incidents Slack channel is on fire
🚨 ALERT: Production API returning 500s. Deploy by: **maya_dev** at 09:01. Commit message: *add user dashboard finally done*
Maya... did you just push directly to `main`?
I finished the feature so I committed and pushed. That's how it works, right?
**deep breath** You imported a package you hadn't installed on the server. It compiled locally but crashed in production. I'm reverting now. Meeting room in five minutes.
**The #1 Git Rule:** Never commit directly to `main` in a team project. The main branch IS production. It must stay deployable at all times.
📍 Meeting room — Alex at the whiteboard, marker in hand
Think of `main` as the trunk of a tree. Production lives here. It stays stable 24/7. When you want to build something new, you don't carve into the trunk — you grow a branch.
So a branch is like... a copy of the code?

Not quite. Think of it as a **parallel timeline**. Git takes a snapshot of where main is right now and creates a pointer. Your new commits go on that pointer. Main keeps going on its own timeline. Neither affects the other — until *you* choose to merge.
So I can mess things up on my branch and nobody gets hurt?
Exactly. That's the entire point of branching. Your disasters stay local.

**Visual:**
A ─── B ─── C ─── D  ← main (stable)
            └── E ─── F ─── G  ← feature/user-dashboard (your work)

A, B, C = shared history  │  E, F, G = only on your branch
📍 Back at their desks — Alex pulls up the terminal
Let's recreate what you should have done this morning. First, make sure you're on main and it's up to date.

git switch main
git pull origin main
Now create your feature branch.
git switch -c feature/user-dashboard
What's the `-c` for?

Create. Without `-c` it tries to switch to an existing branch. The `feature/` prefix is our team convention — it signals what kind of work it is. We use: `feature/`, `fix/`, `hotfix/`, `chore/`. Descriptive, lowercase, hyphens only.

git branch            # list local branches (* = current)
git branch -a         # list local + remote branches
git switch main       # switch back without creating

sections.title: Your Commits Stay on Your Branch

blocks.v: 📍 Maya is coding on her new branch, 30 minutes later
I made a few commits. How do I know they're on my branch and not on main?
Run this. It'll show you the whole picture.

git log --oneline --graph --all

# Output:
* d4e5f6g (HEAD -> feature/user-dashboard) add dashboard stats widget
* a1b2c3d add dashboard skeleton
* h7i8j9k (origin/main, main) fix: login redirect bug
What's `HEAD`?

HEAD is a pointer to *where you are right now*. It always points to your current branch tip. See how `main` is still back at `h7i8j9k`? Your two commits only exist on `feature/user-dashboard`. Main is untouched.
This is so much better than my morning. I broke nothing!
You're learning fast. Commit often, commit early. Small commits are easy to review and easy to revert if something goes wrong.
📍 Tuesday afternoon — Maya is done with her feature
The feature is done and tested. What do I do now? Just merge into main myself?
Definitely not. Push your branch to the remote, then open a Pull Request.

git push -u origin feature/user-dashboard
# The -u sets upstream tracking
# After this first push: just 'git push' is enough
And a Pull Request is...?

Your formal way of saying: *I'm done, please review this before it enters main*. The team reads your diff, leaves comments, requests changes. Only after approval does someone click Merge — and it should never be the author who clicks it.
So my dashboard from this morning should have gone through a PR before going to main?
Yes. And someone would have caught the missing package in review before it ever touched the server.
**The PR is your safety net.** Code review catches bugs, enforces standards, and spreads knowledge across the team. Treat it as a collaboration tool, not a bureaucratic hurdle.
📍 Wednesday — Maya is updating her branch with the latest from main
ALEX. Git is screaming at me. What is a CONFLICT?
Welcome to the rite of passage. Show me what it says.

$ git merge main
Auto-merging src/users/user.service.ts
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/users/user.service.ts
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit.

$ git status
You have unmerged paths.
  both modified:   src/users/user.service.ts

While you were working on your branch, I pushed changes to the same file on main. Git tried to auto-merge them — same file, different sections. But one part overlapped. Git doesn't know whose version wins. It stops and asks YOU to decide.
So git isn't broken. It's just asking for my opinion?
Exactly. Conflicts aren't errors — they're git being careful. Never panic. Open the file.
📍 Alex pulls Maya's file up on the screen
This is what git put in your file. It looks scary but it's just a labelled comparison.

<<<<<<< HEAD  ← START of YOUR version
  async getProfile(id: string) {
    return this.userRepo.findOne({ where: { id } });
  }
=======  ← SEPARATOR
  async getUser(id: number) {
    return this.userRepo.findOne({ where: { id: +id } });
  }
>>>>>>> main  ← END of THEIR version (incoming from main)
So I choose which one is correct, delete the markers, and save?
Yes. You can keep yours, keep mine, combine both — whatever the correct final code should be. Delete ALL the marker lines. Then:

git add src/users/user.service.ts
git commit  # Git pre-fills the merge commit message

# To abort and start over:
git merge --abort
That's... actually not that bad. I thought the whole repo was broken.
The bigger mistake is rushing the resolution. Always read both versions carefully — sometimes you need to combine logic from both sides, not just pick one.
📍 Thursday — Maya is mid-feature when urgent Slack message arrives

Alex! Tech lead just DM'd me — there's a critical bug on the payments branch that needs fixing NOW. But I'm halfway through a new component and git is saying I can't switch branches because I have uncommitted changes!
Two words: git stash.

git stash          # shelve all your WIP — working tree goes clean
git switch fix/payment-null-crash
# ...fix the bug, commit, push, open PR...
git switch feature/user-dashboard
git stash pop      # restore your WIP exactly where you left off
It remembered my half-finished component perfectly. What IS this magic?
It's a stack. You can stash multiple times. Here's the full toolkit:

git stash                        # stash with auto-name
git stash push -m 'navbar WIP'   # stash with a descriptive name
git stash list                   # see everything stashed
git stash pop                    # restore top stash + remove it
git stash apply stash@{1}        # restore specific stash (keep it in list)
git stash drop stash@{1}         # delete a specific stash
git stash clear                  # delete ALL stashes
**Stash also saves untracked files:** Use `git stash -u` to include new files that haven't been `git add`-ed yet.

sections.title: The Day Alex Force-Pushed to Main

blocks.v: 📍 Friday coffee break — Maya asks about the scar on Alex's career
You keep saying never force-push to a shared branch. Did something happen to you?

...*stares into distance*... Three years ago, I was doing an interactive rebase on my local main to clean up the commit history. I made it perfect. Then I typed `git push --force origin main`. And hit enter.
What happened?

I rewrote 6 months of commit history. Every developer on the team now had a diverged repo — their local commits existed on SHAs that were no longer in the remote's history. We spent 8 hours recovering. My manager had a very quiet, very long conversation with me.

# What I did (never do this to a shared branch)
git push --force origin main  ← REWRITES HISTORY FOR EVERYONE

# What I should have done
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/my-branch
# --force-with-lease only force-pushes IF the remote hasn't changed
# since you last fetched. Someone else pushed? REJECTED — safe.

# When is force-push acceptable?
# ✓ Your own feature branch, after a rebase
# ✓ Nobody else has pulled it yet
# ✗ NEVER to main, develop, or any shared branch
**Hard rule:** Always use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force`. And never force-push to a branch other people use.
📍 Friday afternoon — Maya's face has gone pale
I ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` to undo 3 commits... and now my whole afternoon's work is gone from git log. Is it deleted forever?
Don't panic. Git almost never truly deletes commits. Type this:

git reflog

# Output — a full log of everywhere HEAD has been:
a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
d4e5f6g HEAD@{1}: commit: add dashboard export button
h7i8j9k HEAD@{2}: commit: add chart component
p9q0r1s HEAD@{3}: commit: add stats cards
t2u3v4w HEAD@{4}: checkout: moving from main to feature/user-dashboard
Those are my missing commits! They're all there!
Reflog is a log of every position HEAD has ever been at. Now reset to the last good commit:

git reset --hard d4e5f6g
# Your branch jumps back to that commit — all three are restored
Is there anything git CANNOT undo?

Very few things. Git runs garbage collection only after 30+ days of unreachability. The lesson: whenever you feel uncertain about a destructive command, check `git reflog` first. It's your undo button for everything.
📍 Friday end-of-day — Maya's PR got merged, Alex shows her the cleanup
My PR got merged! What now?
Clean up after yourself. Delete the branch locally and on the remote.

git switch main
git pull origin main                           # get the merged changes
git branch -d feature/user-dashboard           # delete locally (safe)
git push origin --delete feature/user-dashboard # delete on remote
Why bother? It's just a branch.
After 6 months of nobody deleting, you'll have 400 branches. Nobody knows which are active, abandoned, or ancient. And this is our naming system — so you always know what a branch is for:

feature/user-notifications   ← new functionality
fix/login-500-error          ← bug fix
hotfix/payment-null-crash    ← urgent production fix
chore/update-dependencies    ← maintenance, no user impact
docs/api-readme-update       ← documentation only
refactor/extract-auth-middleware ← cleanup, no new behaviour
Lowercase, hyphens, prefix. Got it.
And short but descriptive. `feature/stuff` tells me nothing. `feature/user-email-verification` tells me everything.

sections.title: The Mental Model — Things Alex Wishes He Knew Earlier

blocks.v: 📍 Friday 5:30 PM — wrapping up the week over coffee
So to summarise my week: broke production Monday, learned Git the hard way all week.

You broke production, learned branches, conflicts, stash, reflog, and PRs in 5 days. That's a better git education than most developers get in their first year. The ones who never break prod are the ones who also never push anything.
What's the one mental model you wish you had on day one?

Git is a graph of snapshots. Every commit is a snapshot with a pointer to its parent. A branch is just a sticky note on a commit. HEAD is where you're standing. Merging glues two timelines together. Rebasing replays your timeline onto someone else's. That's it. Everything else is details.

Always branch from an up-to-date `main` — never commit directly to it.
Name branches: `feature/`, `fix/`, `hotfix/`, `chore/` — lowercase, hyphens, descriptive.
Commit often and small — easier to review, easier to revert.
Open a PR. Let someone else click Merge. Code review saves teams.
Merge conflicts are not emergencies — read both versions, choose carefully.
Use `git stash` to park work before switching context.
Never `--force` push to shared branches. Use `--force-with-lease` on your own branches only.
When something goes wrong, `git reflog` before panicking — it logs everywhere HEAD has been.
Delete merged branches: `-d` locally, `--delete` on the remote.
**The golden rule:** `main` is always deployable. Protect it like production — because it is.
📍 Tuesday morning — Jordan's first week, Maya's PR sits open for review

Maya, I'm looking at your PR and I count eight commits: *stuff*, *more stuff*, *fix*, *fix for real*, *ok now*, *last fix i promise*, *whoops*, *done*. And you merged main into your branch twice. The history is a wall of noise.
I just... commit when things compile? Is that wrong?
At my last company we rebased everything. Git log read like a book. One commit per logical change. Clean, bisectable, reviewable.
Jordan isn't wrong about the messy history. But the answer isn't always rebase. We're going to have a conversation. **pulls up a chair**
**Commit history is communication.** Whoever reviews your PR — or debugs a regression in six months — will read your commits. The question is what story you want them to find.
📍 At the whiteboard — Jordan draws, Alex observes
When you merge main into your branch to stay up to date, you get this:

A ── B ── C ── D        ← main
     └── E ── F ── M   ← feature/your-branch (M = merge commit)
Rebase *replays* your commits on top of main instead. The result is linear:

A ── B ── C ── D ── E' ── F'   ← feature (rebased onto D)
                              ← main still points at D
E' and F' — they have apostrophes. Are they different commits?

Yes. Same code changes, new commit hashes. Rebase literally rewrites history — it takes your commits off, moves the base point, and replays them one by one. That last part is important: it replays them *one by one*, which means conflicts can appear per-commit, not all at once.

sections.title: Interactive Rebase — Cleaning Up Before You PR

blocks.v: 📍 Alex takes the keyboard — showing Maya her own PR history

There are two separate uses for rebase. The first is updating your branch from main — Jordan showed you that. The second is cleaning up your *own* commits before you ask anyone to review them. That's interactive rebase.

# Rewrite the last 8 commits — only your local ones
git rebase -i HEAD~8

# Or, rewrite everything since you branched from main:
git rebase -i main
Your editor opens with something like this:

pick a1b2c3 stuff
pick d4e5f6 more stuff
pick g7h8i9 fix
pick j0k1l2 fix for real
pick m3n4o5 ok now
pick p6q7r8 last fix i promise
pick s9t0u1 whoops
pick v2w3x4 done
It's just a text file? I can edit it?
Yes. Change the word at the start of each line to control what happens to that commit. Save and close — git executes your instructions from top to bottom.

sections.title: The Commands: pick, squash, fixup, reword, drop

blocks.v: 📍 Alex runs through each option with Maya's commits as examples
Six commands. You'll use three of them constantly.

pick    → keep the commit exactly as-is
squash  → merge into the commit ABOVE IT and combine messages
fixup   → merge into the commit above, DISCARD this commit's message
reword  → keep the commit but open an editor to rename it
drop    → delete this commit entirely
exec    → run a shell command between commits
So here's how you turn Maya's 8 commits into 2 clean ones:

reword a1b2c3 stuff             ← rename to: feat: add user avatar upload
fixup  d4e5f6 more stuff
fixup  g7h8i9 fix
fixup  j0k1l2 fix for real
pick   m3n4o5 ok now            ← rename to: feat: add avatar preview validation
fixup  p6q7r8 last fix i promise
fixup  s9t0u1 whoops
drop   v2w3x4 done              ← it was empty
So I clean my room before guests arrive. That's what this is.
Exactly. Your reviewers are guests. Let them see the finished work, not the mess you made getting there.
📍 10 minutes later — Maya runs the interactive rebase
OK. I saved the file and closed the editor. It says... *Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/user-avatar*. Let me check the log.

# Before:
$ git log --oneline
v2w3x4 done
s9t0u1 whoops
p6q7r8 last fix i promise
m3n4o5 ok now
j0k1l2 fix for real
g7h8i9 fix
d4e5f6 more stuff
a1b2c3 stuff

# After:
$ git log --oneline
e8f9a0 feat: add avatar preview validation
b5c6d7 feat: add user avatar upload
8 commits became 2. That's... actually satisfying.
Now force-push your branch to update the remote. `git push --force-with-lease`.
Use `--force-with-lease`, not `--force`. It only force-pushes if nobody else has pushed to that branch since you last fetched. Safer.

sections.title: The Other Use: Rebasing Your Branch Onto Main

blocks.v: 📍 Maya asks how to stay in sync with main without those merge commits
Jordan said I shouldn't merge main into my branch. So how do I get the latest changes from main onto mine?
Two options. Merge main in (adds a merge commit), or rebase your branch onto main (linear, no merge commit). Here's the rebase way:

git switch main
git pull origin main              # update main
git switch feature/user-avatar
git rebase main                   # replay your commits on top of updated main

# If conflicts: resolve, then:
git add <resolved-file>
git rebase --continue             # proceed to the next replayed commit
# OR:
git rebase --abort                # give up, go back to where you started
The key difference: with `git merge main` you resolve conflicts once. With `git rebase main` you might resolve conflicts for each commit being replayed. More granular. Often cleaner.
And after rebasing onto main, you'll need to force-push your feature branch because its history changed. That's fine — on your own branch, nobody else has pulled it.

sections.title: The Golden Rule — Never Rebase Shared Branches

blocks.v: 📍 Alex tells the cautionary tale that Jordan already knows
Everything we said about rebase has one hard exception. The Golden Rule: **never rebase a branch that other people have already pulled.**
Why? What happens?

Rebase rewrites commit hashes. If Alice pulled commit `a1b2c3`, then you rebase and it becomes `e8f9a0`, Alice's repo and the remote now have different histories for the same logical commit. When she pulls, git sees two divergent timelines and creates a mess of duplicate commits.

# SAFE to rebase:
✓ Your own feature branch — nobody else has it
✓ Before you open a PR (local history only)

# DANGEROUS to rebase:
✗ main / develop / any branch others pull from
✗ Any branch someone else has checked out
✗ After you've opened a PR and teammates are reviewing

I learned this one the hard way. Rebased a shared release branch. The whole team had to coordinate pulling the new history and deleting their local copies. It was a 2-hour recovery and a very quiet Slack channel for a while.

sections.title: git merge --no-ff — When You Actually Want the Merge Commit

blocks.v: 📍 Alex explains why merge commits aren't always bad

Jordan wants linear history. I don't disagree for feature branches. But when you merge a finished feature INTO main, I actually want a merge commit. It marks the integration point. A year from now, I can see exactly when `feature/user-avatar` landed in production.
...That I'll agree with.
The problem: if your feature branch is only one commit ahead of main, git does a *fast-forward* merge by default — just moves the pointer, no merge commit is created. Use `--no-ff` to force one.

# Without --no-ff (fast-forward — no merge commit)
git merge feature/user-avatar
# A──B──E'──F'  ← no record of the feature branch

# With --no-ff (explicit merge commit)
git merge --no-ff feature/user-avatar
# A──B──E'──F'──M  ← M marks: feature merged here
#     └──────────┘  (branch structure still visible in git log --graph)
Many teams configure GitHub/GitLab to always use **Squash and Merge** or **Merge Commit** as the PR merge strategy, so this is enforced automatically — you never have to remember the flag.
📍 End of the conversation — an unexpected moment of agreement

...Okay. I came in wanting to enforce rebase everywhere. My last team did it and it was great. But they had been doing it for 3 years, everyone knew the workflow, and it was written into the contributing guide.

That's the thing. Rebase vs merge isn't a technical argument. It's a *conventions* argument. Both are valid. The problem is when half the team rebases and half merges and nobody agrees. The mess isn't the commits — it's the lack of a shared standard.
So you two were arguing about the same thing from different directions?
...Yes. Let's go write the CONTRIBUTING.md.
📍 Conference room — the team writes the convention together
Here's what we agreed on. Notice: neither camp won completely.

# Our team convention:
#
# 1. Before opening a PR:
#    git rebase -i main  → squash WIP commits into meaningful units
#
# 2. To stay up to date while working:
#    git rebase main     → replay your branch on top (no merge commits)
#
# 3. When merging a PR into main:
#    GitHub: Squash and Merge  → one clean commit per feature in main
#
# 4. NEVER:
#    git rebase main / develop / any branch others pull from
#    git push --force (without --with-lease) on shared branches
So I should have been using interactive rebase to clean my commits before asking for review. Not merging main in repeatedly.
Yes. And now that you know how, your next PR is going to be a pleasure to review. I'm counting on it.

`git rebase -i HEAD~N` — Clean up your own commits before PR (local branch only)
`git rebase main` — Stay up to date without merge commits (local branch only)
`git merge --no-ff feature/x` — Merge with an explicit commit to mark the integration point
`git push --force-with-lease` — Safe force-push after rebase (checks nobody else pushed)
`git rebase --abort` — Bail out of a rebase cleanly if it gets complicated
`git rebase --continue` — After resolving a conflict, replay the next commit
**The golden rule:** Never rebase any branch that another developer has already pulled. Rebase rewrites history — their copy diverges, and the recovery is painful.
**The real answer:** Pick one convention as a team, document it, and follow it consistently. Rebase-everything and merge-always are both fine. Chaos is not.

title: Who Broke the Build? — git bisect

blocks.v: 📍 Friday, 4:32 PM — the CI dashboard turns red. Deploy pipeline blocked.
🚨 CI FAILED · Branch: main · Test: user.service.spec.ts · Error: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'findOne') · 43 tests failed
Alex, CI is broken. Main is red. Nobody's been touching user.service — this is weird.
It was working this morning. So it broke somewhere in today's commits. Let me check how many we've had.

$ git log --oneline main | head -20
a1b2c3f Add payment retry logic
d4e5f6a Refactor auth middleware
g7h8i9b Update user profile endpoint
j0k1l2c Fix: pagination off-by-one
m3n4o5d Add notification service
p6q7r8e Update TypeORM config
s9t0u1f Bump dependencies
... (298 more commits today)
There are 305 commits since this morning. We're going to check every one?
We're not going to check 305 commits. We're going to check **9**.

sections.title: Why git log Is the Wrong Tool Here

blocks.v: 📍 Maya scans the commit messages, looking for anything suspicious
I'm reading the commit messages... 'Update TypeORM config'? That sounds like it could break the repository mock. But maybe 'Bump dependencies'? Could a package update have done it?

You're guessing. Commit messages lie — or at least they're incomplete. A commit called 'fix pagination' might have touched a shared utility that affects user service too. You can't reason your way to the answer from messages alone on a codebase this size.
So what do we do? Checkout each commit and run tests manually?
Not manually. And not every commit. We use binary search — and git has it built in.
📍 Alex draws the search strategy on the whiteboard

Binary search. You know this from CS — instead of checking every item, you check the middle one. If the middle is fine, the bug is in the second half. If it's broken, the bug is in the first half. Each check eliminates half the remaining candidates.

305 commits to search:
Check #1: commit 152  → broken → bug is in commits 1-152 (153 eliminated)
Check #2: commit 76   → works  → bug is in commits 76-152 (77 eliminated)
Check #3: commit 114  → broken → bug is in commits 76-114 (38 eliminated)
Check #4: commit 95   → works  → bug is in commits 95-114
Check #5: commit 104  → broken → ...
Check #6: commit 99   → works
Check #7: commit 101  → broken
Check #8: commit 100  → works
Check #9: commit 101  ← THE BAD COMMIT. Found it.

305 commits → found in 9 checks. log2(305) ≈ 8.25
And git bisect does this automatically?
It picks the midpoint. You run the test. You tell it good or bad. It picks the next midpoint. Repeat until done.
📍 Alex opens the terminal — Maya watches
Three commands to start. Tell git where the good and bad boundaries are.

git bisect start

# Tell git the current commit is broken
git bisect bad

# Tell git that this morning's tag was good
# (use a commit hash, tag, or branch name)
git bisect good v2.1.0-morning-build

# Output:
# Bisecting: 152 revisions left to test after this (roughly 8 steps)
# [d4e5f6a] Refactor auth middleware
It checked out commit d4e5f6a — the middle of the range?
Exactly. Git is now in bisect mode — your working tree is at that midpoint commit. Run the failing test and tell git what you find.

npm test -- user.service.spec
# → PASS ✓

git bisect good
# Bisecting: 76 revisions left to test (roughly 6 steps)
# [p6q7r8e] Update TypeORM config
152 commits eliminated in one check. It jumped to 'Update TypeORM config' — my original suspect!
📍 6 minutes later — checking commit after commit

$ npm test -- user.service.spec  # at [p6q7r8e] Update TypeORM config
# → FAIL ✗
$ git bisect bad
# Bisecting: 38 revisions left (roughly 5 steps)
# [m3n4o5d] Add notification service

$ npm test -- user.service.spec
# → FAIL ✗
$ git bisect bad
# Bisecting: 19 revisions left (roughly 4 steps)
# [j0k1l2c] Fix: pagination off-by-one

$ npm test -- user.service.spec
# → PASS ✓
$ git bisect good
# Bisecting: 9 revisions left (roughly 3 steps)
# [k8l9m0n] Add health check endpoint

$ npm test -- user.service.spec
# → PASS ✓
$ git bisect good
# Bisecting: 4 revisions left (roughly 2 steps)
# [l1m2n3o] Update notification service imports
Wait — 'Update notification service imports'? That has nothing to do with user service. Why would it break our tests?
That's exactly why we don't trust commit messages. Let's run the test and find out.
📍 2 more checks — and git pinpoints the exact commit

$ npm test -- user.service.spec  # at [l1m2n3o]
# → FAIL ✗
$ git bisect bad
# Bisecting: 1 revision left (roughly 1 step)
# [k9l0m1n] Add notification service circular import fix

$ npm test -- user.service.spec
# → FAIL ✗
$ git bisect bad

# 🎯 Result:
l1m2n3o is the first bad commit
author: Jordan <jordan@company.com>
Date:   Fri Jul 24 14:22:11 2026

    Update notification service imports

    <changed files listed here>
Jordan's commit broke it! And it's about notification imports — because NotificationService was imported by UserService somewhere and his refactor created a circular dependency.
9 checks, 8 minutes, 305 commits. Now clean up bisect and go back to HEAD.
git bisect reset  # return to the original HEAD, exit bisect mode

sections.title: Automating bisect With a Test Script

blocks.v: 📍 Alex shows Maya the fully automated version
We typed `git bisect good/bad` manually each time. But you can hand git a script — it runs it at each step and marks the commit automatically based on exit code.

git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.1.0-morning-build

# Run this — git will check out each midpoint and
# use exit 0 = good, exit non-zero = bad
git bisect run npm test -- user.service.spec --silent

# Git runs fully automatically and prints the culprit
# when it finishes — no manual intervention needed
So I could have just run that one command and gone to make coffee?
Yes. The manual way is good for learning. The automated way is good for Fridays at 4:30 PM.

**Requirement:** Your test command must exit with code 0 on pass and non-zero on failure. Most test runners (Jest, Mocha, pytest) do this by default. Bisect run won't work with a script that always exits 0.
📍 Maya asks how to trace a specific line of code back to its author
What if bisect finds the bad commit, but the commit changed 50 files? I still need to find the exact line that caused the problem.
That's git blame. It annotates every line of a file with the commit and author that last changed it.
Should I be worried about running `git blame` on a colleague's code? It sounds accusatory.

Blame is a historical tool, not an accusation tool. The intent is: who can explain this line to me? — not: who should I blame? Good teams know the difference. Some teams rename it `git praise` as an alias, but that doesn't change git.

sections.title: More Detective Tools in the Toolbox

blocks.v: 📍 Alex shares the broader toolkit for tracking down regressions
Bisect and blame are the big two. But here are a few more that save time regularly:

# Search commit MESSAGES for a keyword:
git log --oneline --grep=notification

# Search for when a specific STRING was added or removed:
git log -S findOne --source --all

# See what changed in a specific commit:
git show l1m2n3o
git show l1m2n3o --stat      # just the file list

# See changes to a specific FILE over time:
git log --follow -p src/users/user.service.ts

# Compare two commits on a specific file:
git diff l1m2n3o j0k1l2c -- src/users/user.service.ts
git log -S searches for when a string appeared or disappeared? That's incredibly useful for tracking down where something got deleted.
It's called the pickaxe. Extremely useful when someone removes an important line without a trace. Pair it with `git log -G` for regex searching.

`git bisect start → git bisect bad → git bisect good ` — begin the binary search
`git bisect run ` — fully automated: git checks commits, runs your script, finds the culprit
`git bisect reset` — always run this when done to return to your original HEAD
`git blame ` — see who last changed every line and in which commit
`git log --grep="keyword"` — search commit messages
`git log -S "string"` — the pickaxe: find when a string was added or removed from the codebase
`git show ` — inspect exactly what a commit changed
**Don't guess from commit messages** — messages describe intent, not full impact. Binary search is faster than intuition on any repo with more than 50 commits.
**Bisect works best with small commits** — another reason to commit often. Smaller units mean the bad commit is easy to pinpoint and easy to revert.

sections.title: PR Review Comment #1 Maya Will Never Forget

blocks.v: 📍 Wednesday morning — Maya opens her first PR review notification

⚠ **PR Review Comment from Alex:** Maya, this PR has three problems. (1) node_modules/ is committed — 47,000 files. (2) package-lock.json has a path specific to your MacBook. (3) There is a file called .env containing your database password and a private API key. This PR cannot be merged. We need to talk.
But I ran git add . and it just... added everything. How was I supposed to know not to add those?
Because .gitignore is supposed to stop you from doing exactly this — and yours was empty. Let me fix the .env situation first because that's urgent, and then I'll show you the full picture.

**The .env file contains real credentials.** Even if the PR is closed immediately, the credentials must be considered compromised. GitHub caches content — bots scan for leaked keys within seconds of a push.
📍 Alex starts with the basics before addressing the crisis
.gitignore tells git which files to pretend don't exist. When you run `git add .`, git skips anything matching a pattern in .gitignore.

# Standard .gitignore for a Node.js project:
node_modules/
dist/
build/
.env
.env.local
.env.*.local
*.log
.DS_Store       # macOS folder metadata
Thumbs.db       # Windows folder metadata
*.orig          # merge conflict backup files
Okay, but here's what I don't get. I added .gitignore now with node_modules/ in it. But when I run `git status`, node_modules is still showing as tracked. Why doesn't it disappear?

.gitignore only prevents *untracked* files from being added. Once a file is already tracked — already in the git history — .gitignore has no effect on it. You have to explicitly tell git to forget it.
📍 Alex demonstrates how to untrack files without deleting them
`git rm --cached` removes a file from git's tracking index without touching the actual file on disk. After this, git treats it as if you never added it.

# Remove a single file from tracking:
git rm --cached .env

# Remove an entire folder recursively:
git rm --cached -r node_modules/

# After removal, add the ignore rules and commit:
# (make sure .gitignore already has .env and node_modules/)
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking node_modules and .env"
So node_modules still exists in my project folder, git just stops watching it from this commit forward?

Exactly. The files stay on your machine — git just stops caring about them. But here's the part you need to hear: node_modules is still in your commit history. Anyone who clones the repo and checks out that commit will see them. History is permanent unless you rewrite it.

sections.title: The .env File Is Already on GitHub — Rotate First

blocks.v: 📍 Alex makes Maya do the most important step before anything else

Stop. Before we scrub the history, before we close the PR — rotate those credentials right now. The API key and database password in that .env file are compromised the moment they touch a remote. Assume they were already seen, even if the PR was open for 30 seconds.
How do I rotate them?

Go to your service provider dashboards — the API key provider, the database host. Revoke the old credentials and generate new ones. Update the new values in your .env *locally*. Inform the team there's a credential rotation happening. Then we fix the history.

**Order of operations:** (1) Rotate credentials → (2) Scrub git history → (3) Force-push cleaned history → (4) Add .env to .gitignore → (5) Brief the team. Skipping step 1 means step 2 is cosmetic only — the leaked key still works.
📍 Alex shows how to permanently remove a file from git history
Two tools exist for scrubbing history. The old one is `git filter-branch` — slow and error-prone. The modern tool is `git filter-repo`. Install it, then run:

# Install:
pip install git-filter-repo

# Remove .env from every commit in history:
git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths

# Result: a brand new set of commit hashes with .env never present
# Now force-push the cleaned history:
git push origin --force-with-lease --all
Will this break everyone else's local repos?

Yes. This is why the team needs to know. After the force-push, everyone else has to delete their local clone and re-clone. Their local history has the old commit hashes — after the rewrite, they diverge from the remote. It's disruptive, which is why you want to avoid ever committing secrets in the first place.
📍 Crisis resolved — Alex teaches Maya the full .gitignore syntax
.gitignore patterns are more powerful than they look.

node_modules/       # trailing slash = directories only
*.log               # wildcard: ignore ALL .log files
!important.log      # ! = exception: track this one despite the wildcard above
dist/               # ignore entire dist/ folder
/config.local.js    # leading slash = only root-level config.local.js
doc/**/*.html       # ** = recursive: ignore .html inside any subfolder of doc/
build-*             # prefix wildcard: ignore build-prod, build-dev, etc.
.env                # exact filename
.env.*              # .env.local, .env.staging, .env.production, etc.
The exclamation mark is for when you want to ignore a whole pattern but keep one specific file?
Exactly. Common use: ignore all config files except the example one so new developers know what shape the config should take.

sections.title: The Global gitignore and the Dry Run

blocks.v: 📍 Alex shares two more tools that prevent repeat incidents

Two last things. First: global gitignore. Some files should never be committed from *any* project on your machine — .DS_Store, editor config files, OS junk. You can define a global ignore file that applies everywhere.

# Set up a global gitignore file (do this once per machine):
git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global

# Then add global patterns:
echo .DS_Store >> ~/.gitignore_global
echo Thumbs.db >> ~/.gitignore_global
echo .idea/ >> ~/.gitignore_global       # JetBrains IDE files
echo .vscode/ >> ~/.gitignore_global     # VS Code workspace files
Second: the dry run. Before every `git add .`, run this first:

git add --dry-run .       # -n also works: git add -n .
# Shows exactly what WOULD be staged — without staging it
# Scan for node_modules/, .env, secrets, binaries before committing
If I had run that this morning I would have seen 47,000 files about to be staged and immediately stopped.
That's the lesson.
📍 Alex shows Maya one more convention — the example file
.env is secret and ignored. But a new developer cloning the repo needs to know what variables are required. So we commit a template — .env.example — with all the keys but no real values.

# .env.example — safe to commit, describes required config
DB_HOST=
DB_PORT=3306
DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
JWT_SECRET=
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=

# Onboarding instruction for new developers:
# cp .env.example .env
# Then fill in real values from the team password manager
So commit the shape, never the values. And .gitignore makes sure I can't accidentally commit .env even if I try.
Correct. Store real secrets in a password manager or secrets vault — not in your code, not in Slack, not in email. Only .env.example goes in the repo.

.gitignore only prevents *untracked* files from being staged — it has no effect on files already in history
`git rm --cached ` — untrack a file without deleting it from disk
`git rm --cached -r node_modules/` — untrack a whole directory
`git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths` — permanently scrub a file from all history
`git add --dry-run .` — preview what would be staged before committing
`git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global` — machine-wide ignore for OS junk
**If secrets are committed: rotate credentials first, then scrub history. In that order, every time.**
Keep an `.env.example` with key names but no values — let developers know what config is needed without exposing real secrets
Use a password manager or secrets vault for real credentials — never store them in the repo, Slack, or email

title: The Robot That Won't Let You Ship Sloppy Code

sections.title: Monday — Something Changed in the Repo

blocks.v: 📍 Monday morning — Alex merged a PR over the weekend. Maya pulls and something feels different.
Alex, I pulled this morning and now `npm install` added some new packages — husky, lint-staged. What are those?
I added git hooks. The repo now has an automated gatekeeper that runs before every commit. You'll notice the difference the next time you try to commit.
Gatekeeper? That sounds ominous.
It's a good kind of ominous. Try making a commit with something that has a lint error and see what happens.
📍 30 minutes later — Maya tries to commit a fix
ALEX. My commit is being rejected. I didn't break anything! Look:

$ git commit -m "fix: update user avatar endpoint"

✔ Preparing lint-staged...
✖ Running tasks for staged files...
  ✖ src/users/user.service.ts — eslint --fix-dry-run
    ✖ ESLint found 3 errors:
      Line 24: Unexpected console.log statement (no-console)
      Line 38: Unused variable 'tempUser' (no-unused-vars)
      Line 67: Missing semicolon (semi)
    ✖ Lint check failed

hint: The commit message hook failed — commit aborted.
The robot found three real issues in your file. It's not wrong.
...A console.log I forgot to remove. An unused variable. A missing semicolon. Those are real. Fine. But couldn't it just warn me and let me commit anyway?
A warning you can ignore is not a guardrail. It's decoration. If it doesn't block, it doesn't work.
📍 Alex explains the mechanism while Maya fixes her lint errors
Git hooks are shell scripts that run automatically at specific points in your git workflow. They live in `.git/hooks/`. You can hook into any git event.

ls .git/hooks/
# pre-commit        ← runs BEFORE the commit is recorded
# commit-msg        ← validates the commit message
# prepare-commit-msg
# post-commit
# pre-push          ← runs BEFORE git push sends data
# pre-rebase
# post-merge
# post-checkout
If a hook exits with a non-zero exit code, git aborts the operation. That's why the commit was blocked — the ESLint check exited with errors. If the hook exits 0, git proceeds.
So they're just shell scripts that run at specific moments and can stop git if they fail?
Exactly. And because they're in `.git/hooks/` — which is NOT committed — historically every developer had to set them up manually. That's why tools like husky exist.

sections.title: husky and lint-staged — The Modern Setup

blocks.v: 📍 Alex shows the configuration that makes hooks automatic for the whole team
Husky manages hooks inside the repo and installs them automatically on `npm install`. Lint-staged makes sure we only lint *staged files* — not the entire codebase on every commit.
And because husky is in package.json and .husky/ is in the repo, anyone who clones and runs npm install gets the hooks automatically?
That's the whole point. The rules travel with the repo. No more manual setup, no more developers opting out because they forgot to copy a script.

sections.title: The commit-msg Hook — Enforcing Message Conventions

blocks.v: 📍 Alex adds a second hook to enforce conventional commit format

The commit-msg hook receives the commit message as its argument and can reject commits that don't follow your convention. We use Conventional Commits — that's what makes changelogs and semantic versioning work automatically.

# Valid conventional commit formats:
feat: add avatar upload to user profile
fix: handle null response from payment API
chore: update TypeORM to v0.3.20
docs: add API authentication guide
refactor: extract auth logic into middleware
test: add unit tests for notification service

# Invalid (hook blocks these):
wip
fix stuff
updated things
Done with the feature
So this is what forced Jordan to rewrite his commit messages when he first joined?
Yes. He was annoyed for two days. Now he writes better commit messages than anyone on the team. Constraints breed craft.

sections.title: The pre-push Hook — Last Line of Defense

blocks.v: 📍 Alex adds a third hook — this one runs before code leaves the machine
Pre-commit runs per commit — fast linting. Pre-push runs once before you push to the remote — slower checks that would be painful to run on every commit, like tests.

# .husky/pre-push
#!/usr/bin/env sh
. "$(dirname -- "$0")/_/husky.sh"
npm test -- --passWithNoTests

# Result:
# git push → tests run → if they pass, push proceeds
# If tests fail → push is blocked before code reaches the remote
So even if I forget to run tests manually, the hook runs them for me before I can push broken code to the team?
Exactly. Willpower runs out. Automation does not. When your tools enforce standards, you stop depending on everyone to remember.

**Hooks run locally — they are not a substitute for CI.** Anyone can bypass them with `--no-verify`. CI runs on the server and cannot be bypassed. Use both: hooks for fast local feedback, CI as the authoritative gate.

sections.title: The One Way to Bypass Hooks (And Why You Shouldn't)

blocks.v: 📍 Maya discovers the escape hatch — Alex explains when it's acceptable
I just found out you can do `git commit --no-verify` to skip all the hooks. That seems like it defeats the whole point?

It does. There are two valid reasons to use it: first, a WIP commit you're saving locally and will squash before the PR, second, a genuine emergency where fixing CI to unblock the team matters more than lint. In all other situations, if you find yourself reaching for `--no-verify`, fix the code instead.

# Skip hooks (use sparingly):
git commit --no-verify -m "wip: temp checkpoint before switching tasks"
git push --no-verify

# If a hook is broken and blocking the whole team:
# Fix the hook. Do not normalise bypassing it.
So it's an emergency exit, not a productivity shortcut.
Exactly. If you find you're using it daily, the hooks are probably configured wrong — the threshold is too strict or too slow. Fix the hooks. Don't bypass them.
📍 Two weeks later — Maya's first PR gets reviewed in record time
Alex, Jordan reviewed my PR in 12 minutes and approved it with zero comments. That has never happened to me before.
Because the hooks eliminated the noise. No lint nitpicks, no formatting debates, no missing semicolons. Jordan only had to think about the actual logic of your code.
I was annoyed at the robot for about three days. Now I think it's the best thing in the repo. Every project I work on after this is getting hooks set up on day one.
That's exactly the right conclusion. Automation doesn't replace skill — it protects it. The robot handles the stuff that doesn't need a brain. You save your brain for the stuff that does.

Hooks are shell scripts in `.git/hooks/` that run at git lifecycle events — not committed by default
`pre-commit` → fast checks per commit (lint, format). `pre-push` → slower checks before push (tests)
`commit-msg` → enforce conventional commit format (feat/fix/chore/docs/refactor)
Husky + lint-staged = hooks that travel with the repo and only run on changed files
`git commit --no-verify` skips all hooks — use only for WIP checkpoints or genuine emergencies
Hooks run locally. CI runs on the server. You need both — hooks for fast feedback, CI as the unbypassable gate
**The payoff:** code reviews shrink from 45 minutes to 12. Reviewers discuss logic, not formatting. The robot handles the boring stuff.
If hooks are failing constantly: the threshold is wrong or they're too slow. Fix the hook configuration — don't bypass them

title: Why `this` Is Never What You Think

sections.title: The Button That Broke the Dashboard

blocks.v: 📍 Maya has been staring at a broken console for 20 minutes

Alex, this makes absolutely no sense. I have a button that calls a method on my object. The method logs `this.username`, but it prints `undefined`. The object has a `username` property. It is right there.

Welcome to `this`. The most misunderstood word in JavaScript. The bug you just hit will follow you for your entire career unless you understand one rule: **in JavaScript, `this` is determined by HOW a function is called, not where it is defined.**
📍 Alex explains the fundamental difference from other languages

In Python and Java, `self` / `this` always refers to the instance the method belongs to. Period. The language sets it when the class is instantiated. In JavaScript, `this` is set at the moment of the *call*. Not when you wrote the function. Not when you attached it. At the call.
So when I passed `user.greet` to addEventListener, it detached the function from the object?

Exactly. You passed a reference to the function, not a bound method. When the browser calls it on a button click, `this` inside the function is the button element — because the button is the thing calling the function.
📍 Alex walks Maya through all four ways `this` gets its value
There are exactly four rules. They apply in priority order. The highest priority wins.
My addEventListener case was Rule 3 but the browser was the one calling the function — not my object — so the dot notation pointed to the button?
Precisely. The DOM calls it as `element.handler()`, so `this` = the element. It has nothing to do with where you wrote the function.
📍 Alex shows the ES6 solution that eliminates most `this` bugs
Arrow functions do not have their own `this`. They inherit it from the enclosing scope at the time they are *defined*. This makes them immune to the call-site problem.
So `const self = this` was the old hack before arrow functions existed?
Yes — or `const that = this`, or `const vm = this`. You will still see it in older codebases. Arrow functions obsoleted all of it.
📍 Arrow functions are not always the answer
Can I just use arrow functions for everything and stop worrying about this?
No — two places where arrow functions actively break `this`:
So the rule is: use arrow functions INSIDE methods for callbacks, use regular functions FOR the methods themselves?
That is the mental model. Object methods and event handlers: regular functions. Callbacks inside methods: arrow functions so you inherit the outer `this`.
📍 Fixing Maya's original button bug properly
Going back to your original bug — when you need to pass a method as a callback but preserve its `this`, use `.bind()`. It returns a new function with `this` permanently locked.
The arrow wrapper is cleaner than .bind(). Why would anyone use .bind()?

Partial application — you can pre-fill some arguments. Also, older React class components used it in the constructor before arrow class fields became standard. In modern code, arrow wrappers and arrow class fields cover 95% of cases.

sections.title: `this` in Class Methods — React and the Constructor Pattern

blocks.v: 📍 Where the bind(this) pattern lives on in class-based code
If you ever read older React code, you will see this pattern in class component constructors — this was the canonical fix before class field arrow functions were introduced.
So class field arrow functions are the modern way to make sure class methods always have the right `this`, without needing constructor binds?
Exactly. The constructor bind pattern is still valid — but class fields are shorter and the intent is clearer. Modern codebases prefer them.

**`this` is set at call time, not definition time** — unlike Python/Java where it is always the instance
**Four rules (priority order):** `new` binding > explicit (.call/.bind/.apply) > implicit (dot notation) > default (window/undefined)
Arrow functions have no own `this` — they inherit from the surrounding scope at definition
Use **regular functions** for object methods and event handlers where you want `this` = the caller
Use **arrow functions** for callbacks inside methods to inherit the method's `this`
`.bind(obj)` returns a new function with `this` locked to `obj` permanently. Arrow wrapper `() => obj.method()` is usually cleaner
Class field arrow functions (`handleClick = () => {}`) are the modern replacement for constructor bind patterns
In strict mode, default `this` is `undefined`, not `window` — which makes bugs crash loudly instead of silently corrupting the global object

title: JavaScript at 3 AM: The Event Loop

sections.title: The API Call That Never Came Back

blocks.v: 📍 Maya is debugging a race condition at 3 AM
Alex, I have a bug that only happens sometimes. I fetch user data, then I try to use it on the next line — but it is undefined half the time.

You have just discovered why JavaScript's execution model is different from every other language you have used. It is not a bug in your code. It is a misunderstanding of when code runs. Let me explain the event loop.

sections.title: JavaScript Is Single-Threaded — And That's the Point

blocks.v: 📍 Alex explains the architecture that makes async work

JavaScript runs on a single thread. One thing at a time, top to bottom. But network calls, timers, and I/O take time — blocking the thread for them would freeze the entire page. So JavaScript offloads those to the browser (or Node.js) and continues executing. When they finish, they queue a callback.
So the fetch starts, JS keeps going, and the .then callback only runs AFTER the current synchronous code finishes?
Exactly. Your `console.log(user)` runs immediately, before the fetch resolves. The callback that sets `user = data` runs later, queued up once the network response arrives.

sections.title: The Callback Era — And Why It Became Hell

blocks.v: 📍 Alex shows the old way of handling async — and its fatal flaw
The original solution was callbacks — pass a function that runs when the async thing finishes. Fine for one level. Catastrophic when you needed to chain async operations.
That looks like a staircase of doom. How do you even know where errors go?
You often don't. That was the problem. This is why Promises were invented — and why async/await came shortly after.
📍 The same waterfall — flattened into a readable chain

A Promise is an object representing a value that may not exist yet. It has three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. You chain `.then()` for success and `.catch()` for errors — once, at the end of the chain.

// Same four-step fetch, with Promises
getUser(userId)
  .then(user => getProfile(user.id))
  .then(profile => getPosts(profile.id))
  .then(posts => getComments(posts[0].id))
  .then(comments => render(user, profile, posts, comments)) // scope issue!
  .catch(err => handleError(err)); // one handler for ALL errors
Wait — on that last .then, user, profile, and posts are not in scope anymore?
Exactly — Promises are better than callbacks, but chaining with multiple values gets awkward. That is the motivation for async/await.

sections.title: async/await — Async That Reads Like Sync

blocks.v: 📍 The same logic, now readable at 3 AM

`async/await` is syntactic sugar over Promises. It does not create new threads or block. Under the hood it is still the event loop, still the same queue — but written in a way that reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code.
And `await` pauses execution until the promise resolves, but only inside the async function — not the whole page?
Correct. `await` suspends the async function and hands control back to the event loop. Everything else on the page keeps running. When the promise resolves, the function resumes where it left off.
📍 Maya encounters the patterns that trip everyone up
Three mistakes I see every time someone first uses async/await:
I have done all three of those. The loop one explains why loading 50 users was taking 10 seconds.
Sequential awaits in a loop: 50 users × 200ms each = 10 seconds. Promise.all: all 50 fire at once, ~200ms total. That is a 50x speedup from one line change.

JavaScript is single-threaded. Async operations (fetch, setTimeout, I/O) are offloaded to the runtime. Their callbacks run later, after the current synchronous code finishes.
Code on the line after a `fetch()` runs before the response arrives — never assume data is available synchronously
Evolution: callbacks → Promises (.then/.catch) → async/await (syntactic sugar over Promises)
`await` suspends the async function and yields to the event loop — it does not block the page
`Promise.all([...promises])` fires all at once and waits for all to resolve — use this instead of sequential awaits in a loop
Always handle errors: `try/catch` inside an async function, or `.catch()` at the end of a Promise chain
Forgetting `await` gives you a Promise object, not the resolved value — a very common first bug

title: null, undefined, NaN, and the Type Coercion Circus

sections.title: The Equation That Should Not Equal True

blocks.v: 📍 Jordan is reviewing Maya's code and finds something impossible
Maya, I found a bug in the discount validator. Check this — you're comparing user input with a loose equality check and it's letting through values that should fail.
I do not understand how `null == false` is false but `'' == false` is true. What is JavaScript doing?
📍 Alex joins the code review to explain what == actually does

The double-equals operator tries to coerce both sides to the same type before comparing. It follows the Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm — a table of special rules that produces counterintuitive results whenever types differ.
So the rule is inconsistent because it was designed to be helpful but ended up being a trap. The fix is to never use ==.
📍 The one rule that prevents 90% of equality bugs
The strict equality operator `===` never coerces. Both sides must be the same type AND the same value. Use it everywhere.
So `value == null` is the only legitimate double-equals? Everything else gets triple-equals?
Correct. Enable the `eqeqeq` ESLint rule and it will flag any == that is not the null check pattern.

sections.title: null vs undefined vs NaN — The Three Absences

blocks.v: 📍 Understanding what each actually means
They each mean something different. Mixing them up causes real bugs.
`typeof NaN === 'number'` is the most cursed thing I have seen this week.

It is a historical mistake that cannot be fixed without breaking the internet. IEEE 754 floating-point defines NaN as a numeric value, and JavaScript inherited that. The lesson: always use `Number.isNaN()`, never the global `isNaN()`.

sections.title: Truthy, Falsy, and the Operator Shortcuts

blocks.v: 📍 The patterns everyone uses without fully understanding them
JavaScript has six falsy values. Everything else is truthy. This powers the short-circuit patterns you see everywhere.
