That `??` vs `||` distinction is why we had a bug in the pricing page where discount amounts of 0 were being replaced by the default. Someone used || instead of ??.

Use `===` everywhere. The only valid `==` is `value == null` to catch both null and undefined at once
**null** = intentional absence (the programmer set it). **undefined** = nothing was assigned. **NaN** = invalid numeric operation
`typeof NaN === 'number'` is a historical bug. Use `Number.isNaN()` not `isNaN()`
`NaN === NaN` is false. NaN is not equal to itself — this is not a JavaScript bug, it is IEEE 754
Six falsy values: `false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `[]`, `{}`, and the string `'false'`
Use `??` (nullish coalescing) instead of `||` for defaults when 0 or empty string are valid values
Use `?.` (optional chaining) to safely access nested properties without null-check chains

sections.title: Monday — 347 Packages to Make a Button

blocks.v: 📍 Monday, 10:15 AM — Jordan opens a fresh project. Alex walks over.
Done. I just `npm install`ed everything we need.
For the landing page?
Yeah. Left-pad, is-odd, is-even, is-array, is-boolean, is-function, is-string —
Jordan. Stop. Why do you have a package to check if something is a string?
Because... the README said it handles edge cases?
`typeof value === "string"` has existed since 1995. We are installing no more packages today.
**npm install does not mean it belongs in your project.** Every dependency is a surface area for vulnerabilities, breaking changes, and unmaintained code.
📍 Alex at the whiteboard, Maya watching
npm is the Node Package Manager. It has three jobs: finding packages in the registry, downloading them into `node_modules`, and tracking what you installed in `package.json`.
So `package.json` is like a shopping list?
Exactly. And `package-lock.json` is the receipt — exact versions of every package *and* every package's package. That's what makes builds reproducible.

# Install a package — saves to dependencies
npm install express

# Install dev-only (testing, build tools)
npm install --save-dev jest

# Install globally (CLI tools)
npm install -g typescript

# Install from package.json (fresh clone)
npm install

# Remove a package
npm uninstall express
**Always commit `package-lock.json`.** Without it, different developers get different package versions. `npm ci` uses it for exact, reproducible installs — use that in CI pipelines.
📍 Maya reading a project's package.json for the first time
What's the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
`dependencies` go into production — your app needs them to run. `devDependencies` are only for local development and CI: testing frameworks, linters, bundlers.
And what does `^4.18.2` mean?
That's a semver range. Caret (`^`) means: accept any version `>=4.18.2 <5.0.0`. Major version stays locked, minor and patch can update.
📍 Jordan broke the build by upgrading a package
I ran `npm update` and now TypeScript is throwing 47 errors.
What version did it jump to?
From `4.9.5` to `5.1.0`. Is that bad?
Major version bump. That's a breaking change by definition. This is why semver exists — you broke the contract.

# MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — the semver contract
# 4  .  18  .  2
# │      │     └── Patch: bug fixes only. Safe to auto-update.
# │      └──────── Minor: new features, backward-compatible. Usually safe.
# └─────────────── Major: breaking changes. Review migration guide first.

# ^ prefix — locks major, allows minor + patch
"express": "^4.18.2"  # allows 4.18.x, 4.19.x ... but NOT 5.x

# ~ prefix — locks major + minor, allows patch only
"express": "~4.18.2"  # allows 4.18.x only

# Exact version — no auto-updates at all
"express": "4.18.2"
**Never run `npm update` without checking the changelog.** Always read the migration guide for major version bumps. Minor updates are usually safe; major versions almost always require code changes.

sections.title: npm Scripts — Your Project's Task Runner

blocks.v: 📍 Maya discovers the scripts section
Wait, I've been typing `./node_modules/.bin/jest` this whole time. I can just write `npm test`?
Yes. npm scripts have access to everything in `node_modules/.bin` automatically. That's half their power.

# Run any script defined in package.json
npm run build
npm run lint
npm run dev

# Special scripts — no "run" needed
npm start    # runs "start" script
npm test     # runs "test" script

# Chain scripts
"build:all": "npm run lint && npm run test && npm run build"

# Pass args to the underlying command (-- separator)
npm test -- --watch
npm test -- --testNamePattern=auth
Can I run scripts before other scripts automatically?
Yes — prefix with `pre` or `post`. `prebuild` runs before `build`, `postbuild` runs after. Great for cleaning the dist folder before every build.

sections.title: The node_modules Problem and What to Do About It

blocks.v: 📍 Jordan tries to zip and email the project folder
Why is this 400MB? I just started the project yesterday.
That's `node_modules`. You never share, commit, or zip that folder.
But how does someone else run it without the packages?
They clone the repo, run `npm install`, and npm downloads everything declared in `package.json`. That's the whole system. The registry stores the packages so you don't have to.

# .gitignore — these should always be in it
node_modules/
dist/
.env
.DS_Store
*.log

# Fresh setup on any machine:
git clone https://github.com/your/repo.git
cd repo
npm install        # installs everything from package-lock.json
npm run dev        # start the dev server

**`npm ci` vs `npm install`:** Use `npm install` locally when you want to update packages. Use `npm ci` in CI/CD — it installs exactly from `package-lock.json` and fails fast if the lockfile is out of sync.

sections.title: Security — npm audit and Why It Matters

blocks.v: 📍 Friday afternoon — Slack pings from the security bot
There's a GitHub security alert on the repo. `critical severity vulnerability`.
Run `npm audit`. It scans every package in your dependency tree — not just the direct ones you installed.

# Check for vulnerabilities
npm audit

# Auto-fix what's safe (minor/patch bumps only)
npm audit fix

# Force-fix including major bumps (read the changelog first!)
npm audit fix --force

# Full JSON report
npm audit --json
It says `npm audit fix` won't fix the critical one automatically.
Because fixing it requires a major version bump, which might break things. Check the advisory, find the patched version, pin it in `package.json`, and test.
**`npm audit fix --force` is a last resort.** It can introduce breaking changes silently. Always read the advisory, understand the fix, and run your tests before merging.

`dependencies` = needed at runtime. `devDependencies` = only for dev/build/test.
`package-lock.json` locks exact versions — always commit it.
Semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — major bumps mean breaking changes.
Use `npm ci` in CI/CD pipelines; `npm install` locally.
Never commit `node_modules/` — add it to `.gitignore`.
Run `npm audit` regularly and fix critical vulnerabilities promptly.
Always check the changelog before upgrading major package versions.

title: The Cloud Is Just Someone Else's Computer (Episode 1)

sections.title: Day One at the Cloud Team

blocks.v: 📍 Maya's first day on the Cloud Platform team. Sam, the team lead, pulls up a chair.
Welcome. First question I ask everyone: what is the cloud?
Um... servers? On the internet?
Exactly. That's literally it. Someone else's physical servers in a data centre you can rent by the minute. The "cloud" part is just that you don't have to own or maintain the hardware.
So all those diagrams with cloud shapes — that's just marketing?
Marketing and abstraction. The abstraction part is actually valuable. You stop thinking about physical machines and start thinking about *capacity*, *services*, and *cost*.
**Cloud computing** = on-demand access to computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking) over the internet, typically billed by usage.

sections.title: Before the Cloud — The Pain of Physical Servers

blocks.v: 📍 Sam sketches a timeline on the whiteboard

Before cloud, a startup that needed a server had to: buy hardware, provision it, configure networking, hire someone to maintain it, and then — if it got popular and they needed more capacity — wait 6 weeks for new hardware to arrive.
What happened when traffic spiked?
The site went down. Or you over-provisioned — buying 10x more hardware than you needed just to handle hypothetical peaks. Then it sat idle 90% of the time.

# The old way
Buy server → $5,000 hardware cost
Wait 2-6 weeks for delivery
Hire sysadmin to rack + configure
Pay ongoing power, cooling, space
Over-provision for traffic spikes
Server sits at 10% utilisation most of the time

# The cloud way
Create EC2 instance → in 60 seconds
Pay $0.08/hour while running
Scale up when traffic spikes
Scale down (or off) when it stops

**Cloud economics:** You trade CapEx (large upfront hardware purchase) for OpEx (small recurring operational cost). This is why even large enterprises moved to cloud — better cash flow and faster iteration.
📍 Maya looks at the team's infrastructure dashboard
We're using AWS, but I keep hearing about Azure and GCP. Are they basically the same?

Same concept, different strengths. AWS is the biggest — most services, most mature, most docs. Azure is the default for Microsoft shops — deep Active Directory and .NET integration. GCP is Google's platform — best for data, ML, and Kubernetes (they invented it).

# AWS (Amazon Web Services) — 200+ services, market leader
# Key: EC2 (compute), S3 (storage), RDS (databases), Lambda (serverless)

# Azure (Microsoft) — best for enterprise Windows/Microsoft orgs
# Key: VM, Blob Storage, Azure SQL, Azure Active Directory

# GCP (Google Cloud Platform) — strongest in data + ML
# Key: Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud Run

# All three offer:
# - Global regions and availability zones
# - Pay-as-you-go pricing
# - Managed services (so you don't maintain the underlying infra)
# - 99.9%+ uptime SLAs
**Multi-cloud and hybrid cloud** are common at enterprises — using more than one provider to avoid vendor lock-in or because different teams chose different clouds over time.

sections.title: Regions and Availability Zones — Why Location Matters

blocks.v: 📍 Maya notices the infrastructure is labelled "us-east-1"
What's a region? And why does the config have "us-east-1" everywhere?

A region is a geographic cluster of data centres. `us-east-1` is Northern Virginia. Within each region there are Availability Zones — separate physical buildings a few miles apart, each with independent power and cooling.
Why does that matter?

If one building loses power, the others keep running. You deploy across multiple AZs so a single hardware failure doesn't take down your service. Same idea as not keeping all your backups in the same building.

# AWS region structure example
us-east-1          # Region: N. Virginia
├── us-east-1a     # Availability Zone A (separate data centre)
├── us-east-1b     # Availability Zone B
├── us-east-1c     # Availability Zone C
└── us-east-1d     # Availability Zone D

# Best practice: deploy across 2+ AZs
# If AZ A fails → AZ B and C still serve traffic

# Choose a region close to your users → lower latency
# Also consider: data residency laws (EU data in EU regions)
**Single-AZ deployments are a production risk.** Any well-architected cloud app deploys across at least two Availability Zones behind a load balancer.

Cloud = renting computing resources from a provider's data centres on demand.
You swap CapEx (hardware purchase) for OpEx (pay-per-use).
The Big Three: AWS (most services), Azure (Microsoft/enterprise), GCP (data/ML).
Regions = geographic clusters. AZs = separate buildings within a region.
Deploy across 2+ AZs to survive hardware failures.
Choose a region close to your users for lower latency, and check data residency laws.

title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: Choose Your Weapon (Episode 2)

blocks.v: 📍 Sam brings a pizza box to the standup. Maya is confused.
I use pizza to explain cloud service models. Bear with me.
This feels like a trap.

Making pizza yourself: you buy ingredients, use your oven. That's on-premise — you own everything. Getting pizza delivered: someone else makes it, you just eat it. That's SaaS. Renting a kitchen: someone provides the oven and space, you cook your own pizza. That's PaaS.
And IaaS?
IaaS is renting raw ingredients and a delivery van. You still have to do most of the work, but someone else buys the truck.
The three service models differ in **how much you manage** vs **how much the provider manages**. More control = more responsibility. Less control = less ops burden.
📍 Maya spins up her first EC2 instance

IaaS gives you raw infrastructure: virtual machines, networking, storage. You get a VM — you're responsible for the OS, the runtime, the middleware, and your app. The provider manages the physical hardware.

# IaaS examples
AWS EC2       # Virtual machines
Azure VMs     # Virtual machines
GCP Compute Engine
DigitalOcean Droplets

# What you manage:
# ✓ Operating system (patching, updates)
# ✓ Runtime (Node.js, Python, Java)
# ✓ Middleware (nginx, database)
# ✓ Your application code
# ✓ Scaling configuration

# What the provider manages:
# ✓ Physical servers
# ✓ Network hardware
# ✓ Data centre facilities
So I have a whole Linux server I need to maintain?
Yes. That's the trade-off: maximum control, maximum responsibility. Ideal when you need fine-grained control or have very specific OS/runtime requirements.
📍 Sam shows Maya how to deploy the same app in 2 commands
PaaS abstracts the infrastructure. You bring your code and app config, the platform handles the OS, runtime, scaling, and often the database engine. You just `git push` and it works.

# PaaS examples
Heroku
Google App Engine
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Azure App Service
Render
Railway

# What you manage:
# ✓ Your application code
# ✓ App configuration
# ✓ Dependencies (package.json)

# What the provider manages:
# ✓ OS and patching
# ✓ Runtime version
# ✓ Load balancing
# ✓ Auto-scaling
# ✓ Health checks

# Deploy example (Heroku)
git push heroku main
# That's it. The platform does the rest.
Why wouldn't everyone use this?
Less control. You can't tune the OS, pick your exact runtime config, or use obscure system libraries. And it's usually more expensive per-unit than raw IaaS for the same workload.
**PaaS is ideal for web apps and APIs** where you want to ship fast without managing infrastructure. Teams that care more about product than ops choose PaaS.
📍 Maya realises she already uses SaaS every day
Wait — Gmail is SaaS? And Slack? And GitHub?
Yes. SaaS is the fully-managed end: you use software over the internet and the provider handles everything — infrastructure, platform, application. You just use the product.

# SaaS examples
Gmail, Outlook           # Email
Slack, Teams             # Communication
GitHub, GitLab           # Version control
Jira, Linear             # Project management
Salesforce               # CRM
Dropbox, Google Drive    # Storage
Shopify                  # E-commerce

# What you manage:
# ✓ Your data and usage
# ✓ User accounts / permissions

# What the provider manages:
# ✓ Everything else

# Your company probably buys SaaS and also BUILDS SaaS products
# (your product is probably someone's SaaS)
The product your team ships is a SaaS product. The tools you use to build it — also SaaS. It's SaaS all the way down.
📍 Maya sees a Lambda function in the codebase and has questions
What's a Lambda? The file says "serverless" but we clearly have servers.

Serverless doesn't mean no servers — it means you don't manage them. You write a function, upload it, and the cloud runs it on-demand when triggered. You pay only for actual invocations — not idle time.

# Serverless / FaaS examples
AWS Lambda
Google Cloud Functions
Azure Functions
Vercel Edge Functions
Cloudflare Workers

# How it works:
# 1. Write a function
# 2. Upload it
# 3. Define a trigger (HTTP request, queue message, cron)
# 4. Cloud runs it on-demand, scales to zero when idle

# Cost model:
# Pay per invocation + execution time in milliseconds
# 0 requests = $0.00 (Lambda free tier: 1M requests/month free)

# Best for:
# - Event-driven tasks (image resize on upload)
# - Infrequent but bursty workloads
# - Webhooks and API integrations

**Cold starts:** Serverless functions that haven't been invoked recently take longer on the first call (50ms–1s). For latency-sensitive endpoints, consider keeping functions warm or using IaaS/PaaS instead.

IaaS = raw VMs. You manage OS, runtime, app. Most control, most responsibility.
PaaS = bring your code. Platform manages OS, runtime, scaling. Less control, less ops.
SaaS = use software over the internet. Provider manages everything. You just use it.
Serverless = functions triggered on-demand. Pay per invocation, scale to zero.
Choose based on how much ops work you want to own vs how much you want abstracted away.
📍 Maya gets pulled into a meeting about a new enterprise client
The client says their legal team won't allow data on public cloud. What does that even mean?

It means we need to talk about deployment models. Not all cloud is the same cloud. "Public cloud" means AWS/GCP/Azure — shared infrastructure you rent. "Private cloud" means dedicated infrastructure, either in their data centre or ours.
How is private cloud different from... just having servers?
Private cloud still uses cloud management software — APIs, dashboards, auto-scaling — but runs on hardware no one else touches. You get cloud agility without shared tenancy.
**The deployment model determines who owns and operates the infrastructure**, not what services it runs. You can run Kubernetes on public cloud, private cloud, or both.
📍 Sam walks Maya through the current infrastructure

We're on public cloud right now. AWS owns the hardware. We rent compute, storage, and networking on-demand. We share physical hardware with other AWS customers — though isolated at the VM/container level.

# Public cloud characteristics
Provider:    AWS / Azure / GCP
Hardware:    Shared (you never see it)
Access:      Internet (+ private links available)
Pricing:     Pay-as-you-go, no upfront cost
Scaling:     Elastic — add capacity in seconds
Maintenance: Provider's problem

# Pros
+ No upfront hardware cost
+ Global reach (deploy near your users)
+ Massive service catalogue
+ Scale up or down instantly

# Cons
- Shared tenancy (compliance concern for some industries)
- Data leaves your physical control
- Costs unpredictable at scale
- Dependent on provider uptime
**Public cloud is the default choice for new projects.** The agility and cost model beat private cloud for most use cases — unless regulatory requirements force otherwise.
📍 Maya reads the compliance requirements from the enterprise client
They require "data sovereignty" and "dedicated hardware for regulated workloads." That sounds expensive.
It is. Private cloud means you run cloud management software on hardware you control — either in your own data centre or a colocation facility. You get cloud-style APIs but zero shared tenancy.

# Private cloud characteristics
Hardware:    Dedicated — yours only
Location:    Your data centre or colocation
Access:      Private network (no public internet exposure)
Pricing:     High upfront CapEx + ongoing OpEx
Scaling:     Limited by physical hardware you've provisioned
Maintenance: Your ops team's problem

# Technologies used to build private cloud:
OpenStack   # Open-source cloud management
VMware vSphere + NSX
Nutanix
Ceph        # Distributed storage

# Typical industries that require private cloud:
# Banking, healthcare, defence, government

**Private cloud doesn't mean more secure by default.** You own the security responsibility fully. Public cloud providers invest billions in physical and software security that most private clouds can't match.
📍 Sam presents the architecture proposal to the enterprise client
Most enterprises end up hybrid: regulated, sensitive data stays on private infrastructure. Everything else — web tier, dev environments, analytics — runs on public cloud.
How do the two sides talk to each other without going over the public internet?
VPN or a dedicated private link — AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect. Encrypted, private connection between your data centre and the cloud provider's network.

# Hybrid cloud architecture
Private Data Centre (your hardware)
├── Patient records DB         ← regulated, stays on-prem
├── Financial transaction logs  ← data residency requirement
└── Legacy mainframe app        ← too expensive to migrate
        │
        │  AWS Direct Connect (private, encrypted link)
        │
Public Cloud (AWS)
├── Web/API tier                ← scales elastically
├── Analytics and reporting     ← uses cloud ML services
├── Dev and staging environments
└── CDN and static assets

**Multi-cloud** = using more than one public cloud provider (e.g., AWS for compute, GCP for ML). Hybrid cloud = mixing public cloud with private/on-prem infrastructure. These are different strategies, often combined.

Public cloud = shared hardware rented from a provider. Elastic, pay-as-you-go, default choice.
Private cloud = dedicated hardware you control. Needed for strict compliance/data sovereignty.
Hybrid cloud = both. Regulated workloads on-prem, everything else on public cloud.
Multi-cloud = multiple public providers (different from hybrid).
Connecting private to public: VPN, AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute.
Private cloud ≠ automatically more secure — you own the full security responsibility.

sections.title: Everything Broke and Nobody Knows Why

blocks.v: 📍 Wednesday 2 PM — The staging environment is unreachable. Maya calls Sam.
The app server can't reach the database. Nothing changed in the code.
Nine times out of ten: networking. Let's check the security groups first.
Security groups? I thought those were a firewall thing.
They are. In cloud, every resource has a virtual firewall attached. If the rules don't explicitly allow a connection, it's blocked. Full stop.

**Cloud networking is deny-by-default.** Nothing talks to anything unless an explicit rule allows it. This is different from traditional on-prem networking where internal traffic is often implicitly trusted.

sections.title: VPC — Your Private Network in the Cloud

blocks.v: 📍 Sam draws a network diagram

A VPC — Virtual Private Cloud — is a logically isolated network that you control inside the cloud provider's infrastructure. Your resources live inside it. Nothing can reach them unless you explicitly open a door.

# VPC structure (AWS example)
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16        # Your private address space
├── Public Subnet: 10.0.1.0/24
│   ├── Load Balancer     ← internet-facing
│   └── Bastion Host      ← SSH jump box
│
├── Private Subnet: 10.0.2.0/24
│   ├── App servers       ← no direct internet access
│   └── Background workers
│
└── Database Subnet: 10.0.3.0/24
    └── RDS instance      ← only app servers can reach this

# Internet Gateway → allows public subnet resources to reach internet
# NAT Gateway → allows private subnet to reach internet (outbound only)
**Subnets are how you segment.** Public subnets face the internet. Private subnets are internal-only. Database subnets have the strictest rules — only your app tier can talk to them.
📍 Sam and Maya trace the broken connection
Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached to individual resources. If you allow inbound port 5432, responses automatically flow back out — you don't need a separate outbound rule.
What are NACLs then?

Network ACLs are stateless firewalls at the subnet level. You have to define rules for both inbound AND outbound explicitly. They're your second line of defence, but Security Groups are where most rules live.

# Security Group — attached to EC2, RDS, Lambda, etc.
Inbound rules:
  Port 80   TCP   0.0.0.0/0       # HTTP from anywhere
  Port 443  TCP   0.0.0.0/0       # HTTPS from anywhere
  Port 5432 TCP   10.0.2.0/24    # PostgreSQL from app subnet only
  Port 22   TCP   10.0.1.10/32   # SSH from bastion host only

Outbound rules:
  All traffic 0.0.0.0/0           # Stateful: responses go automatically

# Network ACL (subnet level, stateless)
Rule 100 ALLOW  Inbound  TCP  443   0.0.0.0/0
Rule 200 ALLOW  Outbound TCP  1024-65535  0.0.0.0/0  # ephemeral ports
**Never open port 22 (SSH) to `0.0.0.0/0` (the whole internet).** Use a bastion host or VPN. An open SSH port is scanned and brute-forced within minutes of exposure.
📍 Maya asks why the app has 3 servers but one URL
We have three app servers, but api.company.com resolves to one IP. How?

A load balancer sits in front. It has one public IP. It distributes incoming requests across your healthy backend instances. If one instance crashes, the load balancer stops sending traffic to it within seconds.

# Load balancer flow
User → api.company.com → DNS → Load Balancer IP
                                    │
                          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
                          ▼         ▼         ▼
                       App 1     App 2     App 3
                    (healthy)  (healthy) (unhealthy — removed)

# Types of load balancers (AWS)
ALB (Application Load Balancer) — HTTP/HTTPS, path-based routing
NLB (Network Load Balancer)    — TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency

# DNS — Route 53 (AWS) maps your domain to the load balancer
A record:     api.company.com → 54.22.11.33 (ALB IP)
CNAME record: www.company.com → api.company.com
**Health checks are critical.** Load balancers continuously probe each backend instance (e.g., GET /health every 30s). If it fails twice, traffic stops going to that instance automatically.

Cloud networking is deny-by-default — nothing connects unless explicitly allowed.
VPC = your private isolated network. Segment with public/private/database subnets.
Security Groups = stateful firewall per-resource. Most access rules live here.
NACLs = stateless firewall per-subnet. Second layer, more complex to manage.
Load balancer = distributes traffic, removes unhealthy instances, gives you one entry point.
Never open SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0 — use a bastion host or VPN.
Health checks let load balancers automatically route around failures.

title: Where Does Your Data Actually Go? (Episode 5)

blocks.v: 📍 A user-uploaded video is crashing the API server with memory errors
The upload endpoint downloads the whole file into memory before saving it. For a 2GB video that's... bad.
You don't save files to your server's disk in cloud. You stream them directly to object storage — S3. The server never holds the bytes.
Why not just use the server's filesystem like a normal computer?

Because cloud VMs are ephemeral. They can be replaced, auto-scaled, or terminated. If you save a file to disk on VM #1, VM #2 and VM #3 can't see it. Shared storage is the only thing all instances can access.
**Never write user-uploaded files to a cloud VM's local filesystem.** The file will disappear when the VM is replaced or scaled down. Always use a shared storage service (S3, Blob Storage, GCS).
📍 Sam demonstrates the S3 upload pattern

Object storage is the simplest cloud storage: put a file in, get a URL back. That's it. No filesystem, no directories — just buckets and keys. AWS calls it S3, Azure calls it Blob Storage, GCP calls it Cloud Storage.

# S3 concepts
Bucket:  top-level container (like a hard drive, globally unique name)
Key:     the file path within the bucket
Object:  the file + metadata

# Example
Bucket:  company-uploads-prod
Key:     videos/2026/07/user-123/intro.mp4
URL:     https://company-uploads-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/videos/2026/07/user-123/intro.mp4

# Cost model
# Storage: ~$0.023 per GB/month
# Requests: $0.0004 per 1,000 GET requests
# Data transfer out: $0.09 per GB (the expensive part)

# Key features
# - 11 9's of durability (99.999999999%)
# - Versioning — keep old versions of files
# - Lifecycle rules — auto-move to cheaper storage after N days
# - Presigned URLs — temporary access to private files

**Presigned URLs** let you give temporary access to a private file without exposing your credentials. Generate a URL server-side with a 15-minute expiry, give it to the client. The client uploads/downloads directly to S3 — your server never touches the bytes.
📍 Maya wonders why the database server has a separate disk
The DB instance has an EBS volume attached. What's EBS?

EBS — Elastic Block Store — is cloud block storage. Think of it like a USB drive you plug into a VM. The OS sees it as a regular disk. It persists even if the VM terminates, and you can detach it and reattach to a different VM.

# Storage types

# Block Storage — like a hard drive attached to a VM
AWS EBS
Azure Managed Disks
GCP Persistent Disk
Use case: OS volumes, databases, anything needing a filesystem

# Object Storage — files with URLs, no filesystem
AWS S3
Azure Blob Storage
GCP Cloud Storage
Use case: media uploads, backups, static website hosting, data lakes

# File Storage — shared filesystem, multiple VMs can mount it simultaneously
AWS EFS (Elastic File System)
Azure Files
GCP Filestore
Use case: shared config files, legacy apps that need a shared drive

# In-memory cache — ultra-fast, ephemeral
AWS ElastiCache (Redis/Memcached)
Azure Cache for Redis
Use case: session data, API response caching, leaderboards

sections.title: Managed Databases vs Running Your Own

blocks.v: 📍 The team debates whether to use RDS or run PostgreSQL on an EC2
Why are we paying for RDS when we could just run PostgreSQL on an EC2 instance?

Because RDS gives you automated backups, point-in-time recovery, failover, read replicas, and OS patching — all without touching a single config file. Running your own database on EC2 means your team does all of that. At 3am when production is down.

# Managed database services (examples)
AWS RDS         — Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server
AWS Aurora      — AWS-optimised MySQL/Postgres, ~5x faster, auto-scaling storage
AWS DynamoDB    — NoSQL, key-value, serverless
Azure SQL       — Managed SQL Server
GCP Cloud SQL   — Postgres, MySQL
GCP Spanner     — Globally distributed SQL (very expensive)
MongoDB Atlas   — Managed MongoDB

# What you get with managed databases
# ✓ Automated daily backups + point-in-time recovery
# ✓ Automatic failover to standby replica (Multi-AZ)
# ✓ OS and engine patching handled by provider
# ✓ Read replicas for scaling reads
# ✓ Encryption at rest and in transit
# ✓ CloudWatch metrics out of the box
The cost difference between RDS and EC2+self-managed is often smaller than you think when you price in the engineering time for backups, patching, and incident response.

Never write user uploads to a VM's local disk — it disappears when the VM is replaced.
Object storage (S3, Blob Storage, GCS): files with URLs, 11 9s durability, cheapest at scale.
Block storage (EBS): attached to VMs like a disk, needed for databases and OS volumes.
File storage (EFS): shared filesystem mounted by multiple VMs simultaneously.
Use presigned URLs to let clients upload/download directly to S3 — your server stays light.
Managed databases (RDS, Aurora) handle backups, failover, and patching automatically.

sections.title: The API Key in the GitHub Repo

blocks.v: 📍 Monday morning — GitHub security alert in the team Slack
GitHub found an AWS access key committed to the public repo. From Jordan. Three weeks ago.
How much did it cost us?
$2,400 in EC2 charges. Someone was mining crypto.
Step one: revoke the key now, not after this meeting. Step two: we're going to talk about IAM so this never happens again.

**Leaked AWS credentials are weaponised within minutes.** Bots continuously scan GitHub, Pastebin, and public S3 buckets for access keys. Revoke immediately and audit the past 90 days of CloudTrail logs when this happens.
📍 Sam opens the AWS IAM console
IAM is the foundation of cloud security. Every API call to AWS is an action by an identity — a user, a role, or a service. IAM defines what each identity is allowed to do.

# IAM building blocks

# Users — human or service accounts with long-lived credentials
# Avoid: use roles instead wherever possible

# Groups — collections of users, attach policies to the group
Developers group → ReadOnlyAccess to production
DevOps group    → Full access to EC2, RDS

# Roles — temporary credentials, assumed by services or users
EC2 instance role   → can read from S3 bucket X only
Lambda function role → can write to DynamoDB table Y only
CI/CD pipeline role  → can push to ECR, deploy to ECS

# Policies — JSON documents defining permissions
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
}

**Principle of Least Privilege:** every identity should have the minimum permissions needed to do its job — nothing more. A Lambda that reads from one DynamoDB table should only have permission to read that one table.

sections.title: Roles Over Keys — The Right Way to Give Services Access

blocks.v: 📍 Sam shows Maya how the app server accesses S3 without any access keys in the code
If we can't put access keys in environment variables, how does the EC2 instance access S3?

You attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance. The AWS SDK on the instance automatically picks up temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. No key in code, no key in config. The credentials rotate automatically every hour.
**For local development:** use `aws configure` to store credentials in `~/.aws/credentials`. Never commit that file. Use named profiles to switch between accounts.

sections.title: Encryption at Rest and In Transit

blocks.v: 📍 Compliance audit checklist lands on Maya's desk
The audit form asks if data is encrypted "at rest" and "in transit". What's the difference?
"In transit" means encrypted while it's moving over the network — HTTPS, TLS. "At rest" means encrypted while it's sitting on disk — the database files, the S3 objects, the EBS volume.

# Encryption in transit
# - Use HTTPS (TLS 1.2+) for all public endpoints
# - RDS connections: require SSL (ssl-mode=require in connection string)
# - S3: requests must use HTTPS (enforce with bucket policy)
# - Internal services: mutual TLS or VPC-only communication

# Encryption at rest
# - S3: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed keys) is on by default since 2023
# - EBS volumes: enable encryption at creation (or default to encrypted)
# - RDS: enable encryption when creating the instance (cannot be added after)
# - DynamoDB: encrypted by default, no action needed

# KMS — Key Management Service
# AWS manages the encryption keys for you
# Or bring your own keys (CMK) for compliance requirements
# Audit every key usage in CloudTrail

**RDS and EBS encryption cannot be enabled after creation.** Enable it at launch time. Migrating an unencrypted database to encrypted requires creating a new encrypted snapshot and restoring it — plan this in advance.

Never commit AWS credentials to code or version control — rotate immediately if you do.
IAM: Users for humans, Roles for services. Attach roles to EC2/Lambda — no hardcoded keys.
Principle of Least Privilege: grant the minimum permissions required, nothing more.
The AWS SDK automatically fetches role credentials from instance metadata — no keys in code.
Encryption in transit: HTTPS/TLS for all connections. Enforce it, don't assume it.
Encryption at rest: enable on RDS and EBS at creation — cannot be added later.
Audit access with CloudTrail — every API call is logged.
📍 Monday morning — Maya's first day on the backend team. Sam hands her the README.
I followed every step in the README. Node version matches, dependencies installed. But the API throws an error on startup that nobody else is getting.
What OS are you on?
Windows. The rest of the team is on Mac.
There it is. The README was written on a Mac. You're hitting a path separator issue that only exists on Windows. This is exactly the problem Docker was invented to solve.
**"It works on my machine"** is not a shipping strategy. If your app only runs correctly in one specific environment, you have an environment problem, not a code problem.
📍 Sam opens a whiteboard sketch
A container is a lightweight, isolated process that packages your app together with everything it needs to run — OS libraries, runtime version, config — sealed into one unit.
So it's like a virtual machine?

Similar idea, very different implementation. A VM emulates an entire computer, including a full OS kernel — heavy, slow to start. A container shares the host OS kernel but isolates the filesystem, processes, and network. It starts in milliseconds and uses a fraction of the RAM.

# Rough comparison
VM:
  boots full OS (minutes, GBs of RAM)
  complete hardware emulation
  strong isolation (different kernel)

Container:
  shares host kernel (seconds to start, MBs of RAM)
  isolated filesystem + process tree
  runs identically on any machine with Docker
So a container is: my app + its exact environment, sealed up and guaranteed to run the same everywhere?
Exactly. Build it once, run it anywhere — dev laptop, CI server, production cloud.
📍 Sam explains the two core concepts before touching any commands

Two terms you need to keep separate. An **Image** is the frozen blueprint — your app and its environment, packaged. A **Container** is a running instance of an image. You can run ten containers from one image simultaneously.

# Pull an official image from Docker Hub
docker pull node:20-alpine

# Run a container from that image
docker run node:20-alpine node --version
# v20.x.x — same version, on any machine

# Run interactively (get a shell inside the container)
docker run -it node:20-alpine sh

# Run your app — map port 3000 inside the container → port 3000 on your machine
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-api

# See all running containers
docker ps

# Stop a container
docker stop <container-id>
So `docker run` means: take this image, start a container from it, run this command inside it?
Correct. The image is the blueprint. The container is the running building. The blueprint stays unchanged no matter how many buildings you make from it.
📍 Sam shows how an image is defined and built
You define your own image in a file called `Dockerfile`. It's a recipe: start from a base image, copy your code, install dependencies, define the startup command.

# Dockerfile for a Node.js API
FROM node:20-alpine        # start from the official Node image

WORKDIR /app               # all commands run from /app inside the container

COPY package*.json ./      # copy package files first (cache trick — see Episode 2)
RUN npm ci                 # install dependencies

COPY . .                   # copy the rest of the source code

EXPOSE 3000                # document the port the app listens on
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]  # command that starts the app
Why copy `package.json` before copying all the source files?

Layer caching — Docker caches each step. If you copy source first, any code change forces `npm install` to re-run. Copy package files first and `npm install` only re-runs when dependencies actually change. We'll go deep on this in Episode 2.
Build your image with `docker build -t my-api .` (the `.` means use the current directory as context). The `-t` flag names the image.

**"It works on my machine"** is an environment problem — containers eliminate it
A container packages your app + its exact runtime environment into one portable, reproducible unit
**Image** = frozen blueprint. **Container** = a running instance of that blueprint
Containers share the host OS kernel — far lighter than VMs (milliseconds to start, MBs of RAM)
Define your image in a `Dockerfile`: FROM → WORKDIR → COPY → RUN → CMD
`docker build -t name .` builds an image; `docker run -p HOST:CONTAINER name` runs it
`docker ps` lists running containers; `docker stop <id>` stops one
Images are hosted on registries (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry). `docker pull` fetches them

title: The Image That Weighed More Than the App (Episode 2)

blocks.v: 📍 Maya pushes her first Docker image to the registry. Sam checks the size.
Done! Image is pushed.
Maya. Your Node.js API image is 4.1 GB.
...Is that a lot?

The entire app is 3 MB of compiled JavaScript. You've wrapped it in a 4 GB container. Pulling this in CI takes four minutes. In production, scaling up a new instance takes four minutes. Every extra megabyte is latency and cost.
A bloated image slows CI pipelines, increases cold-start time during auto-scaling, and widens your attack surface. Every library you ship is a potential vulnerability you're responsible for patching.

sections.title: Why It's So Big — Layers and Bad Habits

blocks.v: 📍 Sam pulls up Maya's Dockerfile
Your base image is `node:20`. That includes the full Debian OS, build tools, and compilers — everything used to *build* Node itself. You only need the runtime to *run* your app.

# Maya's original Dockerfile
FROM node:20               # ← full Debian + Node: ~1.1 GB base

WORKDIR /app
COPY . .                   # ← copies node_modules from your laptop too!
RUN npm install            # ← installs deps again on top of what was just copied

CMD ["node", "src/main.js"]
I copied `node_modules` from my local machine AND installed them again inside the container?

Yes. Your local `node_modules` — with native binaries built for your Mac — are baked in alongside a fresh Linux install. Two copies of dependencies, wrong platform binaries. Always add `node_modules` to `.dockerignore`.

# .dockerignore — exclude these from COPY
node_modules
dist
.env
*.log
.git
.github
📍 Sam rewrites the Dockerfile from scratch
Three rules for a slim production image: Alpine base, `.dockerignore`, production-only deps.

# Slimmed Dockerfile — result: ~170 MB instead of 4 GB
FROM node:20-alpine        # ← Alpine Linux: ~5 MB base, no build tools

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev      # ← production deps only, skip devDependencies

COPY dist/ ./dist/         # ← copy compiled output only, not source

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
What does `--omit=dev` do?
It tells npm to skip devDependencies — TypeScript, jest, eslint, all of it. None of those run in production. Why ship a TypeScript compiler into your production container?
Three rules for small images: (1) Use `-alpine` base variants, (2) `.dockerignore` your local build artifacts, (3) `npm ci --omit=dev` for production deps only.

sections.title: Multi-Stage Builds — Compile Inside, Ship Less

blocks.v: 📍 Sam shows the final form: multi-stage builds
If you need build tools to compile the app but not to run it, use a multi-stage build. One stage compiles. The final stage copies only the output — no compiler, no source code, no devDeps.

# Multi-stage Dockerfile

# Stage 1: build (this stage is discarded after)
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                       # install ALL deps — TypeScript compiler included
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                # compile TypeScript → dist/

# Stage 2: production image (only this ships)
FROM node:20-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # production deps only
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist   # copy compiled output from stage 1
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

# Result: ~150 MB. No TypeScript. No source. No devDeps.
So the builder stage is a temporary workspace — TypeScript compiler and all — and the final image only gets what the app needs at runtime?
Exactly. `COPY --from=builder` is how you reach across stage boundaries. The builder is discarded. Only the compiled output crosses into the production image.
📍 Maya notices her rebuilds are slow even after slimming the image
Every time I change a single line of code, the build takes three minutes. It's reinstalling all dependencies every time.
The layer cache is invalidated from the point of the first change downward. If you copy source code before running `npm install`, any code change invalidates the install cache.

# ✗ Wrong order — code change invalidates npm install
COPY . .                   # ← any code change hits this
RUN npm ci                 # ← re-runs on every code change

# ✓ Right order — code change only invalidates COPY . .
COPY package*.json ./      # ← only changes when package.json changes
RUN npm ci                 # ← cached unless dependencies changed
COPY . .                   # ← code changes hit only here

# The rule: put things that change rarely before things that change often
# docker history my-api   ← shows all layers and their sizes
So the Dockerfile is like a waterfall — a change at step N invalidates the cache for all steps after N?
Exactly that. Every COPY, RUN, and ADD creates a new layer. Order those layers from least-to-most-frequently-changing.

Image size affects CI speed, scaling time, cold starts, and attack surface — keep it minimal
`node:20-alpine` vs. `node:20` (Debian): Alpine is ~5 MB base vs. ~300 MB — always use Alpine for production
**Always** create `.dockerignore` — exclude `node_modules`, `.env`, `.git`, `dist`, `*.log`
`npm ci --omit=dev` skips devDependencies — TypeScript, jest, eslint don't belong in production
**Multi-stage builds**: one stage to compile (with build tools), copy only the output into the final stage
**Layer cache order**: `package.json` → `npm install` → source code. Never copy source before installing deps
`docker history <image>` shows every layer and its size — use it to find bloat
Smaller images = smaller attack surface. Unused libraries are CVEs you're shipping.

title: One Command to Rule Them All (Episode 3)

blocks.v: 📍 Jordan joins the team. The onboarding doc is three pages long.
The README says: start Redis on port 6379, start Postgres on 5432, run the migration script, set fourteen environment variables, then start the API. In that exact order. Some steps have footnotes.
How long did it take?
Three hours. Redis was on the wrong version so the cache middleware crashed. I had to uninstall and reinstall it. The migration script errored because Postgres wasn't fully ready yet.
We're replacing all of that with one command.

A setup process that depends on things starting in the right order, with the right versions, on the right OS, is a process that will fail for every new hire, every CI machine, and every developer who reinstalls their laptop.
📍 Sam opens the compose.yml file on the screen
Docker Compose defines your entire local stack — API, database, cache — in one YAML file. One command starts everything in the right order, connected, with the right environment variables.

# compose.yml
services:
  api:
    build: .                    # build from local Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/appdb
      - REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy    # wait for DB health check, not just startup
      cache:
        condition: service_started

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data   # data persists across restarts
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U user"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"

volumes:
  pg_data:
`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` — that means the API won't start until Postgres actually passes its health check? Not just when the container starts?
Correct. The old way: start everything and hope the DB is ready before the API tries to connect. The Compose way: wait until it's actually healthy.

sections.title: The Commands You'll Use Every Day

blocks.v: 📍 Jordan tries it for the first time

# Start everything (builds images if needed, then starts)
docker compose up

# Start in background (detached — logs not shown)
docker compose up -d

# Rebuild images and start (use after Dockerfile changes)
docker compose up --build

# Stop all services (containers stop, data in volumes survives)
docker compose stop

# Stop AND remove containers (volumes survive)
docker compose down

# Stop AND remove containers + volumes (wipes database data)
docker compose down -v

# Stream logs from all services
docker compose logs -f

# Stream logs from one service only
docker compose logs -f api

# Run a one-off command inside a running service
docker compose exec db psql -U user -d appdb
What's the difference between `stop`, `down`, and `down -v`?

`stop` pauses the containers — everything restores on `up`. `down` removes the containers but leaves your volumes — data is safe. `down -v` also removes volumes. Use it when you want a completely clean slate — like resetting your local database from scratch.
Never run `down -v` carelessly on a shared or staging environment. It drops all volume data — the equivalent of running DROP DATABASE. Fine locally. Catastrophic on anything shared.

sections.title: Networking — How Services Find Each Other

blocks.v: 📍 Jordan wonders why the API uses 'db' not 'localhost'
In the compose file the database URL says `@db:5432`. But on my laptop Postgres is at `localhost:5432`. What is `db`?

Compose creates a private network and puts all services on it automatically. Inside that network, each service is reachable by its service name — `db`, `cache`, `api`. From inside the API container, `localhost` means the API container itself.

# From inside the 'api' container:

# ✓ correct — use the service name defined in compose.yml
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/appdb
REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379

# ✗ wrong — 'localhost' inside the api container means the api container
#   not the db container
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/appdb

# From your host machine (laptop):
# Reach services through the published ports:
# Postgres: localhost:5432   (because compose.yml has ports: 5432:5432)
# Redis:    localhost:6379
# API:      localhost:3000
So each container has its own localhost — and to talk to another container you use its service name from compose.yml?
Exactly. Compose handles the DNS automatically. You just use the name you defined in the file.

You only need to publish ports (the `ports:` key) for services you want to reach from your laptop — like the API or a DB GUI. Service-to-service traffic (API → DB) stays on the internal network and needs no published ports.

Docker Compose defines your entire local stack (API + DB + cache + ...) in one `compose.yml`
`docker compose up` starts everything; `up -d` in background; `up --build` rebuilds images first
`docker compose down` removes containers — volumes survive. `down -v` also removes volumes (wipes data)
`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` waits for the health check, not just container start
Services talk to each other using their service name (`db`, `cache`) — not `localhost`
`docker compose logs -f <service>` streams live logs from a specific service
`docker compose exec <service> <cmd>` runs a command inside a running container (e.g., `psql`, `redis-cli`)
For CI and onboarding, `docker compose up` should be the only setup step needed

title: The Force Push That Rewrote Everyone's History (Episode 6)

blocks.v: 📍 Tuesday afternoon. Jordan rebased a feature branch to clean up commits before the PR.
I rebased my branch to squash those WIP commits. Git says my branch has diverged from origin. How do I push?
What branch is it?
feature/user-auth. I just ran `git push --force` to sync it up.
Did anyone else have that branch checked out?
...Maya was reviewing it and pulling updates to test locally. Why?
Because you just rewrote the history that Maya's local copy is based on. Her branch now points to commits that no longer exist on origin.
📍 Alex explains at the whiteboard
When you rebase, git creates brand new commits with new hashes — even if the content is identical. The old commits still exist on Maya's machine, but origin now has completely different history.

# Before rebase — Jordan and Maya both had:
A → B → C → D  (feature/user-auth on origin)

# Jordan rebased and squashed:
A → B → E       (E is a new commit with a new hash)

# Jordan force-pushed:
# Origin now: A → B → E

# Maya's local still has:
A → B → C → D   ← these commits no longer exist on origin

# Maya tries to pull:
$ git pull
error: Your branch and 'origin/feature/user-auth' have diverged
# Maya's local history is now orphaned from the remote
So every commit I had locally, based on C and D — those are now stranded? They don't exist on origin anymore?
Stranded is the right word. You can recover — but everyone who had the branch has to do a hard reset or cherry-pick. Which is exactly why we don't force-push to shared branches.
**Never `git push --force` to a branch that other people have checked out.** You rewrite shared history and everyone else's local copy becomes invalid.
📍 Alex shows the alternative that should always be used instead
`--force-with-lease` only lets the push through if nobody has pushed new commits to that branch since you last fetched. It refuses to overwrite work you haven't seen.

# What Jordan ran:
git push --force              # ← overwrites origin regardless of what's there

# What Jordan should have run:
git push --force-with-lease   # ← fails if someone else pushed commits you haven't fetched

# Example: someone pushed while you were rebasing
$ git push --force-with-lease
error: failed to push some refs
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work
hint: that you do not have locally.
# ← this refusal is exactly what you want — it saved you from overwriting their work

# To resolve: fetch, rebase onto the latest, then try again
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/feature/user-auth
git push --force-with-lease
So `--force-with-lease` is: force-push, but only if I haven't missed any commits from someone else?
Exactly. It protects against the most common force-push accident: overwriting commits you didn't know existed.
Alias `--force-with-lease` or set it as your default in `.gitconfig`. There is almost no scenario where bare `--force` is the correct answer.

sections.title: The Rule — When Force Push Is Actually OK

blocks.v: 📍 Alex gives Jordan the complete policy
Force-pushing isn't always wrong. It's wrong on shared branches. On your own branches, it's a normal part of cleaning up history before a PR.

# ✓ SAFE — your own feature branch, only you have it
git rebase -i HEAD~3           # squash and clean up commits locally
git push --force-with-lease    # safe-force to update the remote

# ✓ SAFE — cleaning up a branch before opening a PR
#   (do this before others start reviewing, not after)

# ✗ NEVER — force push to main or develop
git push --force origin main   # this is how careers end

# ✗ NEVER — force push while someone is actively reviewing
#   (it resets their local and invalidates PR comment line numbers)
#   Coordinate first: squash only before the PR, or after explicit agreement
So the rule is: force-push is fine on your own branches before others are involved. Once it's shared — coordinate.

And always `--force-with-lease`, not `--force`. Most teams also configure branch protection rules on `main` that block force-pushes entirely at the repo level — making this mistake physically impossible on the important branches.

Rebasing creates new commit hashes — even for identical content. Force-pushing after a rebase on a shared branch strands everyone else's local copy
`--force` overwrites origin unconditionally — use this almost never
`--force-with-lease` fails if someone pushed commits you haven't fetched — always use this instead
Force-push is acceptable on **your own solo feature branch** before others are involved
Never force-push to `main`, `develop`, or any branch with active reviewers without coordinating
If you force-pushed and broke someone's branch: `git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/<branch>`
Branch protection rules on `main` make force-pushing physically impossible — configure this on your repo
📍 Friday afternoon. Alex and Maya both finished their features and are trying to merge.
ALEX. I tried to merge my branch and git is showing me a conflict. It says there are 23 conflicting files.
23. That is a large number. How long has your branch been open?
...Three weeks?
And you haven't pulled main in three weeks.
No.
OK. Here's what happened and here's how we fix it.

**Merge conflicts grow with branch age.** A branch open for three days has small, isolated conflicts. Three weeks means conflicts across every file anyone on the team touched. Merge or rebase onto main frequently — at minimum every few days.
📍 Alex opens the first conflicting file
Git marks exactly where the conflict is. The markers show you both versions — your branch and theirs — side by side. You must choose what the final code should look like.

<<<<<<< HEAD (current branch — main)
const timeout = 5000;
=======
const timeout = 30000; // increased for slow network environments
>>>>>>> feature/maya-auth

# The three parts:
# <<<<<<< HEAD      ← YOUR version (the branch you're merging INTO)
# =======           ← divider between the two versions
# >>>>>>> branch    ← THEIR version (the branch being merged in)
So `HEAD` is main — the branch I'm merging into — and the bottom is my feature branch?

Yes. And you have to decide: keep mine, keep theirs, or write something new that combines both. Git will not make that call for you. Every conflict marker in every file must be manually resolved and removed before the merge commit can complete.
📍 Working through the files one by one
Three outcomes: take one side, take both, or write something new. The right choice depends entirely on what the code does. Read both versions before deciding.

# Case 1: Take theirs — Maya's change was correct
const timeout = 30000; // increased for slow network environments
# Delete the markers and the other version

# Case 2: Take mine — main's version was correct
const timeout = 5000;
# Delete the markers and the other version

# Case 3: Both are right — they serve different purposes
const DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5000;
const NETWORK_TIMEOUT = 30000; // slow network environments
# Keep both, remove all markers

# After resolving each file:
git add src/config/timeouts.ts   # marks this file as resolved

# After all conflicting files are resolved:
git commit                        # completes the merge
# Git pre-fills the merge commit message — you can edit or accept it
So: open each conflicting file, delete all the markers, keep only the right code, then `git add` it?
Exactly. A file that still has `<<<<<<<` markers in it cannot be committed — git will refuse. `git add` is how you tell git: this file is resolved.

Use `git mergetool` or your editor's built-in UI for large conflicts. VS Code shows a three-way view — yours, theirs, and the merged result — which is much easier to reason about than raw markers in a text file.
📍 Two hours later, all conflicts are resolved. Alex gives Maya the real lesson.
You resolved 23 conflicts. Good. Here's how you make sure this never happens again.

# Pull main into your feature branch regularly — at least every few days
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main       # or: git merge origin/main

# Before opening a PR: always rebase onto latest main first
# Resolve any conflicts locally so the PR shows a clean merge

# Check what diverged between your branch and main
git diff main...feature/maya-auth

# See only which files are different
git diff --name-only main...feature/maya-auth

# If things go wrong mid-merge, abort and go back to clean state:
git merge --abort
# or, if rebasing:
git rebase --abort
So I should be rebasing onto main every few days — not waiting until the entire feature is done?
Yes. Three-week-old branches are archaeology projects. Three-day-old branches are a five-minute rebase. The longer you wait, the more the world has moved on from where you branched off.

Conflicts happen when two branches edit the same lines — git cannot auto-resolve them
`<<<<<<< HEAD` is your current branch, `>>>>>>> branch` is the incoming, `=======` divides them
For each conflict: remove the markers, keep the correct code, then `git add` the file
`git commit` (after all files resolved) completes the merge
`git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` cancels mid-process and returns to a clean state
`git mergetool` and editor-integrated UIs make large conflicts much easier to navigate
**Prevention**: rebase onto main frequently — daily on active branches — to keep conflicts small
Open PRs early, keep branches short-lived. Long-running branches are the root cause of nightmare merges
📍 Thursday, 2 PM. Maya is halfway through a feature refactor when Slack pings.
The payment API is returning 500 errors for all users in production. Someone needs to fix it now.
Can you take it?
I'm in the middle of refactoring the auth module. Half my files are changed, nothing compiles. I can't commit this half-broken state.
You don't need to commit it. Use `git stash`.

`git stash` saves your uncommitted changes to a temporary shelf and restores a clean working directory — without making a commit. Your work is safely stored and you can switch branches or start a hotfix immediately.
📍 Alex walks Maya through the full workflow

# 1. Save all uncommitted changes to the stash
git stash
# Saved working directory and index state WIP on feature/auth: a3b2c1d

# Your working directory is now clean — as if you never started
git status
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

# 2. Switch to main and create the hotfix branch
git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix/payment-500

# 3. Fix the bug, commit, push, open PR — normal workflow
git add src/payment/payment.service.ts
git commit -m "fix: resolve 500 on payment endpoint"
git push origin hotfix/payment-500

# 4. Return to your feature branch
git checkout feature/auth

# 5. Restore your stashed work — exactly as you left it
git stash pop
# Your half-finished auth refactor is back
And `stash pop` restores everything — modified files, new files, deleted files, all of it?
Everything you had uncommitted at the time of the stash. It's a precise snapshot of your working directory state at that moment.
📍 Maya has been stashing things all week without naming them
I stashed something two days ago and I have no idea what it was. Is it still there?
Stash is a stack. Everything you've stashed is still there until you explicitly pop or drop it.

# List all stashes
git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on feature/auth: a3b2c1d Refactoring auth module
# stash@{1}: WIP on feature/dashboard: 9f8e7d6 Dashboard layout
# stash@{2}: WIP on main: 1a2b3c4 Some experiment

# See what's actually in a specific stash
git stash show -p stash@{1}

# Restore a specific stash (not just the most recent)
git stash apply stash@{1}    # apply but keep the stash entry
git stash pop stash@{1}      # apply AND remove from the list

# Delete a stash you no longer need
git stash drop stash@{2}

# Delete ALL stashes
git stash clear

# Name your stashes so the list is readable:
git stash push -m 'half-done auth refactor'
What's the difference between `apply` and `pop`?
`pop` applies the stash and removes it from the list. `apply` restores the changes but leaves the stash entry — useful if you want to apply the same stash to multiple branches or keep it as a backup.
Always name your stashes with `-m`: `git stash push -m 'description'`. WIP labels are meaningless after two days. A named stash tells you exactly what you'll get back.
📍 Maya tries to pop a stash and hits a conflict
I ran `git stash pop` and got a conflict. The same file was changed by someone else while I was working on the hotfix.
Stash pop applies your saved changes on top of the current state. If the same lines changed on both sides — your stash and the current branch — you get a conflict, same as a merge.

# If stash pop produces conflicts:
# 1. Resolve the conflicting files (remove markers, keep correct code)
# 2. Stage the resolved files
git add src/auth/auth.service.ts

# IMPORTANT: when stash pop fails mid-way, the stash entry is NOT removed
# After resolving, manually drop it:
git stash drop

# Alternative — cleaner escape hatch:
git stash branch recovery/stashed-auth stash@{0}
# Creates a new branch from the exact commit where you stashed,
# then pops the stash onto it — no conflicts because the base is identical
# Work from there and open a PR when ready
So `git stash branch` creates a branch at the exact commit where I stashed — meaning the stash applies cleanly with no conflicts?
Yes. It's the cleanest way out when a stash conflicts badly with the current state of the branch.

`git stash` saves all uncommitted changes to a stack and restores a clean working directory
`git stash pop` restores the most recent stash and removes it from the list
`git stash apply` restores without removing — useful when applying one stash to multiple branches
`git stash list` shows all saved stashes; `git stash show -p stash@{N}` shows the diff
`git stash push -m 'name'` names your stash — do this; WIP messages are useless after two days
`git stash drop stash@{N}` deletes one stash; `git stash clear` deletes all
Stash pop can conflict — resolve like a merge conflict, then `git stash drop` manually
`git stash branch <name>` is the escape hatch when conflicts are too messy — creates a branch at the stash point and pops cleanly

title: The S3 Bucket That Was Open to the World (Episode 1)

blocks.v: 📍 Maya is building a file-upload feature and needs her uploads accessible via URL.
I just need the uploaded images to be publicly readable so the frontend can display them. There's a checkbox in the S3 console called "Block Public Access." I unchecked it. It's only for testing.
When did you do this?
Two days ago. Why?

Our security scanner just flagged your bucket as publicly enumerable. That means anyone on the internet can list every file in it and download all of them. Including the user profile uploads from production.
...It was just for testing.

**Public S3 buckets have been the source of some of the largest data breaches in cloud history.** Turning off Block Public Access makes the entire bucket — including files you didn't intend to expose — readable and listable by anyone with an internet connection.
📍 Sam shows Maya what "publicly enumerable" actually means

S3 has two levels of access control. The first is the Block Public Access setting — a master switch. The second is individual ACLs and bucket policies. When you unchecked Block Public Access, you removed the safety net.

# Anyone can now list every object in the bucket:
curl https://your-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2

# Response shows every key (filename) in the bucket:
<Key>users/1/profile.jpg</Key>
<Key>users/2/profile.jpg</Key>
<Key>users/2/id-scan-front.jpg</Key>   ← government ID, now public
<Key>users/3/payslip-2024-01.pdf</Key> ← payslip, now public

# And each file is directly downloadable:
curl https://your-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/users/2/id-scan-front.jpg
# 200 OK — file downloaded, no auth required
They can see the filenames just from the list endpoint. And then just download them.
No credentials required. S3 buckets are globally addressable. Once public, they're public to the whole internet, not just your team.

sections.title: Block Public Access — The Master Switch

blocks.v: 📍 Sam re-enables Block Public Access and explains what each setting does
AWS added Block Public Access as a separate override because people kept granting public access by accident through ACLs and policies. It's a master kill switch that wins over everything else.

# The 4 Block Public Access settings (all should be ON for most buckets):

BlockPublicAcls:        true  # reject any request that grants public ACL
IgnorePublicAcls:       true  # ignore any existing public ACLs already on objects
BlockPublicPolicy:      true  # reject bucket policies that allow public access
RestrictPublicBuckets:  true  # restrict public and cross-account access

# To set via AWS CLI:
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket your-bucket-name \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

# AWS now turns ALL FOUR on by default for new buckets.
# If you inherited old buckets, audit them:
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket your-bucket-name
So even if I accidentally write a bucket policy that grants public access, BlockPublicPolicy=true will just reject it?
Yes. It's the safety net under the safety net. Turn all four on and never touch them unless you have a very specific reason.
AWS S3 Block Public Access is now enabled by default on new buckets (since April 2023). Always verify inherited or migrated buckets — legacy accounts often have this disabled.

sections.title: Serving Files Without a Public Bucket

blocks.v: 📍 Maya still needs the frontend to display uploaded images — Sam shows the right way
OK but I still need users to be able to see their uploaded profile photos. If the bucket is private, how does the browser load them?

Two patterns. For short-lived URLs, use Pre-Signed URLs. For long-lived public content, put CloudFront in front of S3 with an Origin Access Control — only CloudFront can read the bucket, not the public.
So the browser never talks directly to S3. It talks to my API, which generates a signed URL, which expires.

For user-specific files — profile photos, documents — yes. Signed URLs give you per-user, per-file, time-limited access with a full audit trail. For truly public assets like a marketing site's images, CloudFront is the right layer.

S3 buckets with Block Public Access disabled are accessible to anyone on the internet — including file listing
AWS enables Block Public Access (all 4 settings) by default on new buckets — audit legacy buckets
Never disable Block Public Access "just for testing" — use pre-signed URLs or CloudFront instead
**Pre-signed URLs**: your backend generates a time-limited URL for a specific object — no public bucket needed
**CloudFront + OAC**: CDN sits in front of S3, only CloudFront can read the bucket — best for static assets
S3 access logging: enable on every bucket to record who accessed what and when
IAM bucket policies control cross-account and programmatic access — keep them scoped to specific actions and prefixes
For the CLF-C02 exam: S3 storage classes (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier) and the shared responsibility model (AWS secures the infrastructure; you configure access correctly)

title: The Bill That Gave Everyone a Heart Attack (Episode 2)

sections.title: The Email Nobody Wanted to Open

blocks.v: 📍 Monday morning. Maya opens her email and freezes.
Sam. Our AWS bill this month is twelve thousand dollars. Last month it was two hundred.
Which account?
The production account. We only have one.
Was there a traffic spike? A new service launched? Anything unusual?
Nothing. Same traffic as always.
Then something is running that shouldn't be. Let's find it.

A bill that jumps 60x month-over-month with no traffic increase is almost always one of three things: a forgotten resource left running, a data transfer charge nobody planned for, or a Free Tier expiry that nobody tracked.

sections.title: Finding the Culprit with Cost Explorer

blocks.v: 📍 Sam opens AWS Cost Explorer — Billing → Cost Explorer in the console
Cost Explorer shows your spend broken down by service, region, account, and tag. First step: group by service and find what exploded.

# Cost Explorer walkthrough:
# 1. AWS Console → Billing → Cost Explorer
# 2. Set date range: last 3 months
# 3. Group by: Service
# Result this month:
#   EC2-Other (data transfer):  $9,200   ← WAT
#   EC2 Instances:              $1,100
#   RDS:                        $900
#   Everything else:            $800

# "EC2-Other" is the category for NAT Gateway and data transfer charges
# Drill down: Group by → Usage Type
#   DataTransfer-Out-Bytes:     $7,400   ← 74 TB of data transferred out
#   NatGateway-Hours:           $1,800   ← NAT Gateway nobody turned off

# Find the forgotten NAT Gateway:
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --query "NatGateways[*].{ID:NatGatewayId,State:State,Created:CreateTime}"
We have a NAT Gateway from the VPC setup two months ago that nobody deleted. And something transferred 74 TB out of our account?

Check the S3 bucket we just secured. Someone might have been downloading all our files before we locked it down. Data transfer OUT of AWS to the internet is always charged — there is no free tier for egress.
📍 Sam explains the Free Tier fine print that nobody reads
The AWS Free Tier catches almost every new team. Here are the traps that generate surprise bills.

# Trap 1: "750 hours/month" is per account, not per instance
# If you run 2x t2.micro instances: 2 × 744h = 1,488h → you pay for the extra 738h
# Free Tier only covers ONE t2.micro or t3.micro running 24/7

# Trap 2: Data transfer OUT is always charged
# Free Tier: 100 GB/month out to the internet
# After that: ~$0.09/GB depending on region
# 74 TB = 74,000 GB × $0.09 = $6,660 in transfer alone

# Trap 3: Free Tier expires after 12 months
# RDS, EC2, Elastic IPs — all free for year 1, then full price on month 13
# Nobody sets a calendar reminder for this

# Trap 4: Elastic IPs cost money when NOT attached
# 1 Elastic IP per running instance = free
# Any unattached Elastic IP = $0.005/hour ($3.60/month each)
# You had 12 unattached IPs from old test servers = $43/month

# Trap 5: NAT Gateways are expensive to forget
# $0.045/hour + $0.045/GB processed
# One forgotten NAT Gateway = $32/month before any traffic
We had 12 unattached Elastic IPs from old experiments?
Every time someone spun up a test EC2, clicked "allocate Elastic IP," then deleted the instance but not the IP. Twelve months of that adds up.
Run AWS Trusted Advisor regularly. It flags idle resources, unattached Elastic IPs, underutilized instances, and open security groups — all for free on any account.

sections.title: Budgets and Alerts — Never Be Surprised Again

blocks.v: 📍 Sam sets up cost alerts so this never happens again

AWS Budgets lets you define a spending threshold and get alerted before you hit it. You should have three budgets minimum: a monthly total, a service-specific one for the biggest services, and an anomaly detector.

# AWS Budgets — set up in Billing → Budgets

# Budget 1: Monthly total threshold
Budget name: Monthly-Total
Budget amount: $300/month
Alerts:
  • 50% actual ($150) → email team
  • 80% actual ($240) → email + Slack
  • 100% forecasted ($300) → email + Slack + page on-call

# Budget 2: Service-level alert (catch runaway EC2/data transfer)
Budget name: EC2-Plus-Transfer
Filter by service: EC2, Data Transfer
Amount: $150/month

# Budget 3: Cost Anomaly Detection (catches spikes automatically)
# Billing → Cost Anomaly Detection → Create monitor
# AWS ML detects unusual spend patterns and alerts you
# You set the threshold: alert if anomaly > $50 in a day

# Also: set a CloudWatch billing alarm (older approach, still useful)
# CloudWatch → Alarms → Billing → Create alarm
# EstimatedCharges > $200 → SNS → email
So Budgets sends the alert before the bill arrives, not after?

AWS bills monthly. Without budgets, you find out what you spent 30 days too late. With alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100%, you get three warnings while you still have time to act. Cost Anomaly Detection catches same-day spikes — like that S3 egress event.

AWS Cost Explorer: group by Service to find what's driving spend; drill into Usage Type for detail
Data transfer OUT of AWS to the internet is always charged — there is no free egress
Free Tier traps: 750h/month EC2 is per-account, expires after 12 months, doesn't cover data transfer
Unattached Elastic IPs, idle NAT Gateways, and forgotten snapshots all cost money every hour
Set up AWS Budgets: alert at 50%, 80%, 100% of your monthly threshold — not just 100%
Cost Anomaly Detection catches same-day spending spikes via ML — enable it on every account
Trusted Advisor (free tier) flags idle resources, security issues, and cost optimizations
For the CLF-C02 exam: understand the AWS pricing models (on-demand, reserved, spot, savings plans), Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), and the AWS Free Tier specifics

title: Who Is Allowed to Do What? — IAM (Episode 3)

blocks.v: 📍 Sam gets a security alert from AWS GuardDuty at 11 PM.
Maya. Our Lambda function's AWS credentials were used to create 47 EC2 instances in us-east-1 at 10:58 PM. We don't have any process that does that.
Someone is using our Lambda's credentials?
Yes. And the reason they could spin up 47 EC2 instances is that someone gave that Lambda AdministratorAccess — full permission to do anything in the AWS account. Who set that up?
...I did. It was easier than figuring out the exact permissions it needed.

**AdministratorAccess on any non-human identity is one of the most dangerous configurations in AWS.** If those credentials are leaked — through code, logs, environment variables, or a dependency vulnerability — an attacker has full control of your AWS account.
📍 Sam traces how the credentials were exposed

Lambda functions on AWS should use IAM Roles, not static access keys. Roles provide temporary credentials that rotate automatically. A static access key, once leaked, works forever until manually rotated.

# What Maya did (wrong):
# Created an IAM User "lambda-user"
# Gave it AdministratorAccess
# Generated an Access Key + Secret
# Set them as Lambda environment variables:
#   AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = AKIA...
#   AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = ...

# How it leaked:
$ git log --all --full-history -- .env
commit a1b2c3d  (6 months ago)
    "initial setup"
# The .env was committed once, deleted in the next commit
# But git history keeps it forever — anyone who clones the repo can see it

# The attacker found it with:
git log --all -p | grep "AWS_SECRET"

# What Maya should have done:
# Create an IAM Role with only the permissions Lambda needs
# Assign the role to the Lambda function
# Lambda gets auto-rotating temporary credentials — no key files, no secrets
The .env was deleted from the repo but it's still in the git history?

Git never forgets. `git rm` removes the file from future commits, not from history. If a secret was ever committed, assume it's compromised. Rotate it immediately and then scrub the history if necessary.
📍 Sam explains the three IAM building blocks

IAM has three main concepts. Users are for humans — people who log into the console or use the CLI. Roles are for services — EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks. Policies are the JSON documents that define what actions are allowed.
So a policy is literally a list of: which actions, on which resources, are allowed or denied?

Exactly. AWS evaluates these policies on every API call. Default is deny. An action is only allowed if a policy explicitly permits it. The structure is: Effect + Action + Resource. Master those three fields and you can read any IAM policy.
📍 Sam rebuilds the Lambda's permissions the right way
Principle of least privilege: give every identity only the permissions it needs for its exact job, nothing more. Start with nothing, add what is required.

# Step 1: Create an IAM Role for the Lambda (not a User)
# In console: IAM → Roles → Create Role → Lambda → attach policy

# Step 2: Write a scoped policy — only what this Lambda actually does
# Lambda reads from input-bucket and writes to output-bucket:
{
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::input-bucket/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject","s3:PutObjectAcl"],
