      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::output-bucket/*" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["logs:CreateLogGroup","logs:PutLogEvents","logs:CreateLogStream"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:*:*:*" }
  ]
}

# Step 3: Assign the role to Lambda — no access keys needed at all
# Lambda automatically gets temporary credentials that rotate every hour
# If the code is leaked, the temporary credentials expire and are useless

# Additional must-dos:
# - Enable MFA on every human IAM user
# - Never use the root account for daily work
# - Create billing alerts on the root account only
# - Root account should have no access keys at all
The Lambda uses the role and gets temp credentials automatically. There are no keys to leak, no secrets in environment variables.

And if someone breaks into the Lambda container and dumps the environment, they get credentials that expire in an hour. The blast radius is contained. That's what least privilege actually buys you — limited time and limited scope when something goes wrong.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources in your account that are accessible from outside your organization. It catches overly-permissive S3 buckets, IAM roles, and KMS keys automatically.

IAM Users = human identities. IAM Roles = service identities (Lambda, EC2, ECS). Never use a User for a service.
A policy is: Effect (Allow/Deny) + Action (what API calls) + Resource (which ARNs). Default is Deny.
Roles provide auto-rotating temporary credentials — no static access keys, nothing to leak
Never commit AWS credentials to git. Even deleted files live in git history forever.
Principle of least privilege: grant only the actions and resources the identity actually needs
Never use the root account for daily work — lock it with MFA and delete its access keys
IAM Access Analyzer and GuardDuty detect misconfigured permissions and suspicious activity automatically
For CLF-C02: understand Shared Responsibility Model (AWS secures the cloud, you secure access within it), IAM users/groups/roles/policies, MFA, and the principle of least privilege

title: The EC2 That Never Stopped Running (Episode 4)

blocks.v: 📍 Sam reviews the team's AWS architecture for the first time
Walk me through the production setup.

One EC2 instance. t2.xlarge. It runs the API, the background job processor, the file conversion worker, and Redis. It's been running since we launched eighteen months ago. We just restart it when it crashes.
You're running 24/7 at maximum capacity for a workload that peaks for two hours a day.
The rest of the day it's at about 8% CPU.
And you're paying full price for 100% capacity, 24 hours a day, to use 8% of it for 22 of those hours. Let's talk about what EC2 can actually do.

A single large EC2 instance running everything 24/7 is the most expensive way to use AWS. It combines the worst of both worlds: you pay for peak capacity during off-peak hours, and you have no redundancy if it goes down.
📍 Sam opens the EC2 instance type comparison
EC2 has hundreds of instance types organised into families. Each family is optimised for a different workload. Picking the right family saves money without losing performance.

# EC2 instance type families
t  (General Purpose, Burstable)   — t3.micro, t3.small, t3.medium
   Best for: APIs, small web apps, dev environments
   Earns CPU credits when idle, uses them when busy

m  (General Purpose, Balanced)    — m6i.large, m6i.xlarge
   Best for: application servers, databases with mixed load

c  (Compute Optimised)            — c6i.large, c6i.xlarge
   Best for: CPU-intensive: video encoding, scientific compute

r  (Memory Optimised)             — r6i.large, r6i.xlarge
   Best for: in-memory databases, large caches, data analytics

g  (GPU Instances)                — g4dn.xlarge, p3.2xlarge
   Best for: ML training, video transcoding, graphics rendering

# Current setup: t2.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) = $0.1856/hour = $134/month
# CloudWatch shows: avg CPU 8%, avg memory 3 GB used
# Right-sized: t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM) = $0.0416/hour = $30/month
# Savings: $104/month (78%) for the same actual workload
We're paying for 16 GB of RAM and using 3 GB. And 4 CPUs and using less than one.
AWS CloudWatch → EC2 → Metrics will show you your actual average utilization over the last month. Right-size first, then think about scaling. You cannot fix inefficiency by scaling.
AWS Compute Optimizer analyses your CloudWatch metrics and recommends right-sized instances. It's free to use and often finds 40-70% savings on over-provisioned instances.

sections.title: Auto Scaling — Match Capacity to Demand

blocks.v: 📍 Sam introduces Auto Scaling Groups
Instead of one large instance running at 8% all day, run a fleet of small instances that scales up during peak hours and back down when traffic drops. You pay only for what you use.

# Auto Scaling Group (ASG) — the core construct
Min capacity:     1   # always at least 1 instance running
Desired capacity: 2   # start with 2
Max capacity:     10  # never scale beyond 10

# Scaling policy — Target Tracking (simplest)
Target: CPUUtilization = 50%
# If average CPU goes above 50% → add instances
# If average CPU goes below 50% → remove instances
# AWS handles the math automatically

# What happens in practice:
# 2 AM (quiet):   1 instance running, CPU 12%
# 9 AM (peak):    4 instances running, CPU 48%
# 12 PM (lunch):  6 instances running, CPU 52%
# 6 PM (evening): 2 instances running, CPU 30%

# Behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB):
# ALB distributes traffic across all healthy instances
# When ASG launches a new instance, ALB automatically includes it
# When an instance fails its health check, ALB stops routing to it
# and ASG replaces it with a fresh one automatically
So if one instance crashes, the load balancer stops sending it traffic and the auto scaler replaces it. The users barely notice?
Correct. You get redundancy and elasticity in one setup. The single EC2 you have now is a single point of failure — one crash, everything is down until you restart it manually.
📍 Sam explains the three pricing models — the biggest lever on your EC2 bill
How you pay for EC2 matters as much as which instance you pick. Three models exist, each suited to different workloads.

# On-Demand: pay per second, no commitment
# Price: full rate
# Use for: variable workloads, testing, short-lived jobs
t3.medium on-demand: $0.0416/hr = $30/month

# Reserved Instances: 1 or 3-year commitment, large discount
# Price: up to 72% off on-demand
# Use for: steady baseline load you know you'll always need
# 1-year t3.medium Reserved (no upfront): $0.026/hr = $19/month (37% off)
# 3-year t3.medium Reserved (all upfront): ~$0.016/hr = $12/month (62% off)
# Note: Savings Plans are a more flexible alternative to Reserved Instances

# Spot Instances: unused AWS capacity, deep discount, can be interrupted
# Price: up to 90% off on-demand — price fluctuates by supply/demand
# Use for: batch processing, data analytics, ML training, stateless workers
# t3.medium Spot: ~$0.012/hr = $8.60/month (79% off)
# Catch: AWS can reclaim Spot instances with 2-minute warning

# Practical strategy:
# Min instances in ASG → Reserved (stable baseline)
# Scale-out instances during peaks → On-Demand or Spot (burst capacity)
# Batch jobs, background workers → Spot (fault-tolerant by design)
So we should run the minimum number of instances as Reserved, and let Auto Scaling add On-Demand or Spot for spikes?
Exactly. That's the well-architected cost model: commit to your floor, flex your ceiling, use Spot for interruptible work. Most mature teams save 50-65% on EC2 with this combination.

EC2 instance families: t (burstable), m (balanced), c (compute), r (memory), g (GPU) — pick the family that matches your workload
Right-size before scaling: check CloudWatch CPU and memory averages over 30 days, then drop to the smallest instance that handles your actual load
Auto Scaling Groups: set min/max/desired, attach a Target Tracking policy — AWS handles scale-in/out automatically
Application Load Balancer in front of ASG: distributes traffic, health-checks instances, replaces unhealthy ones
On-Demand: flexible, full price. Reserved: 1-3 year commit, 37-72% off. Spot: interruptible, up to 90% off
Savings Plans are a flexible alternative to Reserved Instances — commit to a $/hour spend, not a specific instance type
AWS Compute Optimizer analyses your usage and recommends right-sized instances for free
For CLF-C02: know the EC2 purchase options, Auto Scaling concepts, and Elastic Load Balancing types (ALB, NLB, CLB)

sections.title: The Image Resizer That Ran All Night

blocks.v: 📍 Sam reviews the services list and spots something
What is "image-resize-server" — t3.small, running 24/7 since March?
Users upload photos. We resize them to thumbnails on the backend. The server listens for new uploads and processes them.
How many photos get uploaded per day on average?
About four. Sometimes ten on a busy day.
So this t3.small runs for 86,400 seconds every day to do about 40 seconds of actual work.
I mean... it has to be ready when an upload comes in.
Lambda disagrees with that premise.
When a service sits idle 99.9% of the time waiting for occasional events, you're paying for the waiting. Lambda bills only for the execution — zero cost at zero requests.

sections.title: Lambda: A Function, Not a Server

blocks.v: 📍 Sam explains the Lambda mental model
Lambda is Functions-as-a-Service. You write a function, upload it, define what triggers it, and AWS handles everything else. No server to provision, patch, or pay for when idle.
So the function wakes up when a file is uploaded, resizes it, then goes back to sleep. We pay nothing while it's sleeping.
Exactly. And it scales automatically — if 1,000 photos are uploaded simultaneously, Lambda runs 1,000 instances of the function in parallel. No configuration needed.
📍 Sam shows the full range of what can invoke a Lambda
Lambda is event-driven. Almost every AWS service can be a trigger. You define what event fires the function — Lambda handles the wiring.

# Common Lambda triggers:

S3:           New file uploaded → resize, scan, index, notify
API Gateway:  HTTP request arrives → Lambda IS your API endpoint
SQS:          Message in queue → process it (Lambda polls the queue)
SNS:          Notification published → fan out to multiple Lambdas
EventBridge:  Scheduled (cron) → run at 2 AM every night
DynamoDB Streams: Item changed → react to data changes in real time
Cognito:      User signs up → send welcome email, provision resources
CloudFront:   Edge request → Lambda@Edge to customize CDN responses

# Maya's setup:
# S3 trigger: new object in "uploads" bucket → Lambda handler fires
# Cost for 120 invocations/month (Maya's use case):
#   Invocation cost:   $0 (free tier: 1M/month)
#   Duration (512 MB × 3 seconds × 120): 180 GB-seconds
#   Duration cost:     $0.003/month

# vs. t3.small 24/7:
#   $16.20/month
#   Saving: 99.98%
99.98% saving for literally the same work. Because the image resizer was doing nothing for 99.95% of its life.
Lambda is the right tool when your workload is event-driven, unpredictable, or bursty. It's the wrong tool when you need consistent low-latency responses or very long-running processes.
📍 Maya asks about the catch — there's always a catch
This sounds too good. What's the catch?
Cold starts and hard limits. Lambda functions that haven't been invoked recently take longer to execute the first time — AWS has to spin up a container from scratch.

# Cold start: Lambda hasn't been invoked recently
# AWS spins up a new container, loads the runtime, loads your code
# Adds 100ms–1s to the first invocation (varies by runtime and package size)
# Node.js cold start: ~100-300ms
# Java cold start: ~1-3s (JVM startup is slow)
# Python cold start: ~100-200ms

# Cold start mitigation:
# 1. Provisioned Concurrency: keep N containers warm at all times
#    Cost: you pay for the reserved containers even when idle
#    Use for: latency-sensitive, user-facing functions

# 2. Scheduled ping: trigger the function every few minutes
#    Cheap hack, not reliable at scale

# Lambda hard limits (know these for CLF-C02):
# Max execution time:     15 minutes
# Max memory:             128 MB to 10,240 MB (10 GB)
# Deployment package:     50 MB zipped, 250 MB unzipped
# Temp storage (/tmp):    512 MB to 10 GB
# Concurrent executions:  1,000 per region (soft limit, can be raised)

# Lambda is NOT suitable for:
# - Long-running jobs (> 15 min) → use ECS Fargate or EC2
# - Stateful workloads (Lambda is stateless — /tmp is ephemeral)
# - Very consistent high-throughput with strict latency (always-warm EC2 wins)
For the image resizer — cold starts don't matter. A user uploading a photo doesn't care if it takes 300ms extra to generate the thumbnail.
Correct. For async background work, cold starts are irrelevant. For a real-time user-facing API — where every millisecond counts — you'd either use Provisioned Concurrency or a traditional server.

Lambda is Functions-as-a-Service: write a function, define a trigger, pay only per invocation and duration
Free tier: 1 million invocations/month and 400,000 GB-seconds — most low-traffic functions cost nothing
Lambda scales automatically from 0 to 1,000 concurrent executions — no configuration
Triggers: S3, API Gateway, SQS, SNS, EventBridge (cron), DynamoDB Streams, and more
Cold start: 100ms-3s delay when a function hasn't run recently — use Provisioned Concurrency for latency-sensitive functions
Hard limits: 15-minute max runtime, 10 GB memory, 1,000 default concurrent executions per region
Lambda is wrong for: long-running processes (>15 min), stateful workloads, always-on low-latency APIs
For CLF-C02: understand FaaS vs. IaaS vs. PaaS, Lambda triggers, and the serverless cost model (pay per execution, not per hour)
📍 Tuesday morning. Sam opens Slack to a chain of messages from 3 AM.
Maya. Production was down for 43 minutes last night. A user tweeted about it at 3:07 AM. We didn't find out until 3:50 AM when someone on the team happened to check Twitter.
We had no alerts set up. I didn't even know there was a way to get notified about this automatically.

CloudWatch has been silently collecting data about every service we run — CPU, memory, request counts, error rates, latency — since day one. We just never told it to tell us when something went wrong.
Forty-three minutes of downtime that a tweet reported before we did.
Never again. Let's set this up properly.
**Unmonitored infrastructure is infrastructure you don't actually control.** You only learn about problems when users tell you — and users don't file bug reports, they leave.
📍 Sam opens the CloudWatch console and shows what was there all along
CloudWatch Metrics are time-series data points. Every AWS service publishes metrics automatically. EC2, RDS, Lambda, ALB — they're all already reporting. You just haven't been looking.

# Metrics available automatically (no setup required):

# EC2:
CPUUtilization          # % CPU used (most useful)
NetworkIn / NetworkOut  # bytes transferred
StatusCheckFailed       # 1 if instance is unreachable
DiskReadBytes           # I/O activity

# RDS (database):
DatabaseConnections     # active connections
FreeStorageSpace        # bytes remaining (alert before it hits 0)
ReadIOPS / WriteIOPS    # database load
FreeableMemory          # RAM available

# Application Load Balancer:
RequestCount            # requests per minute
HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count  # 500 errors from your app
HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count  # 400 errors (client errors)
TargetResponseTime      # latency in seconds
HealthyHostCount        # how many instances are healthy

# Lambda:
Invocations / Errors    # call volume and error rate
Duration                # execution time in ms
Throttles               # rate-limit hits
ConcurrentExecutions    # simultaneous executions

# Custom metrics: push anything you want
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --namespace "MyApp" \
  --metric-name "ActiveUsers" \
  --value 1423 \
  --unit Count
The ALB already tracks 5XX errors and response time? That would have shown us the outage the moment it started.
It was tracking it. `HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count` spiked to 100% at 3:04 AM. The data was there. We just had no alarm watching it.

sections.title: Alarms — Get Woken Up Before Users Do

blocks.v: 📍 Sam creates the alarms that should have existed from day one
A CloudWatch Alarm watches a metric and fires an action when it crosses a threshold. The action is usually an SNS topic — which sends an email, Slack message, or PagerDuty page.

# Alarm 1: API is returning errors
# Metric: ALB HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
# Threshold: > 5 errors in 1 minute
# Action: SNS → email + Slack webhook
# Why 5 not 0: minor blips happen; 5 consecutive means something is wrong

# Alarm 2: High latency (API is slow, not just erroring)
# Metric: ALB TargetResponseTime
# Threshold: > 2 seconds (p99) for 3 consecutive minutes
# Action: SNS → email

# Alarm 3: Instance is unreachable
# Metric: EC2 StatusCheckFailed
# Threshold: >= 1 for 2 minutes
# Action: SNS → email + PagerDuty (wake someone up)

# Alarm 4: Database running out of space
# Metric: RDS FreeStorageSpace
# Threshold: < 5 GB for 10 minutes
# Action: SNS → email (not urgent yet, but needs attention today)

# Create via CLI:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "API-5XX-Errors" \
  --metric-name HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \
  --statistic Sum \
  --period 60 \
  --threshold 5 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:ops-alerts
If we'd had alarm 3 — StatusCheckFailed — we'd have been paged at 3:04 AM instead of finding out from Twitter at 3:50.
Forty-three minutes faster. And if we'd had alarm 1 watching 5XX errors, we would have caught it even earlier — the errors started spiking 30 seconds before the instance fully failed.

Use **Composite Alarms** to reduce alert fatigue: fire a page only when BOTH error rate AND latency are elevated. A single 5XX spike in isolation is noise. Both metrics bad at the same time means a real incident.
📍 Sam shows how to investigate once an alarm fires
Alarms tell you something is wrong. CloudWatch Logs tell you why. Application logs, system logs, Lambda output — all flow into CloudWatch Logs automatically if you configure the agent.

# CloudWatch Logs Insights — SQL-like query language for logs
# Run in CloudWatch → Logs Insights → select log group

# Find all errors in the last hour:
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50

# Count error types:
fields @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| parse @message "ERROR * *" as errorCode, errorMsg
| stats count(*) as errorCount by errorCode
| sort errorCount desc

# Find slow requests (> 1 second):
fields @timestamp, @duration, @requestId
| filter @duration > 1000
| sort @duration desc
| limit 20

# What caused the 3 AM outage (disk full):
# Found in logs: "ENOSPC: no space left on device"
# RDS FreeStorageSpace was at 0 MB
# Queries failing, connections timing out, API returning 500s

# Fix: RDS storage auto-scaling (enable once, AWS handles it)
aws rds modify-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier prod-db \
  --max-allocated-storage 200   # auto-scale up to 200 GB
  --apply-immediately
The 3 AM outage was the database running out of disk space? That's it?

Yes. Six months of logs accumulating in the database until it hit the storage limit. One alarm on FreeStorageSpace would have given us a week of warning. Enable RDS storage auto-scaling and this never happens again.

**Log retention**: CloudWatch Logs are kept forever by default — and you pay per GB stored. Set a retention policy on every log group: 30 days for debug logs, 90 days for application logs, 1-7 years only for compliance-required logs.

CloudWatch collects metrics from every AWS service automatically — EC2, RDS, ALB, Lambda, and more. The data is there; you just need to watch it.
CloudWatch Alarms: watch a metric, fire an action when it crosses a threshold. Route to SNS → email/Slack/PagerDuty.
Key alarms to create on day one: 5XX error rate (ALB), response time (ALB), StatusCheckFailed (EC2), FreeStorageSpace (RDS)
Composite Alarms combine multiple conditions — reduce noise by alerting only when two signals are both bad simultaneously
CloudWatch Logs Insights: query-based log analysis — find errors, count exceptions, identify slow requests
Set log retention policies — logs kept forever are a cost that grows indefinitely
RDS storage auto-scaling: enable it so the database never runs out of disk mid-night
For CLF-C02: know CloudWatch Metrics vs. CloudWatch Logs vs. CloudWatch Alarms; CloudTrail (API audit trail, who did what) vs. CloudWatch (performance and application monitoring); AWS Config (resource compliance)

title: The Domain They Forgot to Renew (Episode 1)

blocks.v: 📍 Monday, 8 AM. Maya opens Slack to a flood of notifications.
Sam. Our client's website is completely unreachable. They've been getting emails from customers since 2 AM saying the site is gone.
Not a server error — the DNS resolution is failing. Let me check the domain.

# Quick diagnosis: check if domain resolves at all
nslookup clientsite.com
# Result: NXDOMAIN — non-existent domain
# This is not a server problem. The domain itself is gone.

# Check WHOIS to see the registration status:
whois clientsite.com
# Registry Expiry Date: 2026-07-19T00:00:00Z
# Domain Status: redemptionPeriod

# Today is July 22. The domain expired three days ago.
The domain expired. It's been in the redemption period for three days. Auto-renew was off.
They didn't own the domain forever?

Nobody ever owns a domain. You lease it — usually year by year. When the lease runs out and nobody renews, the domain stops working. Every website that goes down without a server issue — this is almost always the cause.
**Domain expiry is one of the most common causes of unexpected website downtime.** A domain that has lapsed takes the entire site, email, and any subdomain services with it instantly.
📍 Sam explains the domain system while they wait on hold with the registrar
A domain name is a human-readable alias for an IP address. Computers use IP addresses — browsers use domain names. The Domain Name System is the global database that maps one to the other.

# Anatomy of a domain:
clientsite   .com
─────────    ────
Second-level  Top-level domain (TLD)
domain (SLD)

# The registrar is the company you lease the domain from:
# Namecheap, GoDaddy, Google Domains (now Squarespace), Cloudflare
# ICANN accredits registrars and manages the TLD registry

# What you're actually renting: the right to control
# the DNS record for that name for the lease period
# Typical price: $8–15/year for .com
# The registrar renews your lease annually (or you can prepay 5–10 years)

# WHOIS: the public registry of domain ownership
whois example.com
# Registrar: Namecheap Inc.
# Registered On: 2018-03-14
# Expires On: 2027-03-14
# Updated On: 2026-02-01
# Registrant: (often privacy-protected)

# Privacy protection (WHOIS privacy / Redacted for Privacy):
# Hides your personal name, email, phone from the public WHOIS record
# Almost all registrars offer it free now — always enable it
So the registrar holds the lease and they need payment every year. What actually happens when it expires?

Three stages. First, the domain stops resolving — the site goes down immediately. Then a 30-day grace period where the original owner can renew at normal price. After that, a redemption period — 30 more days — where you can still get it back but pay a $150-300 recovery fee. After that, it goes to public auction. Squatters bid on expired domains all day long.
📍 While the domain is being recovered, Sam maps out the client's full domain setup
The main domain expiring didn't just take down the website. It took down everything — email, the admin panel, the API, all of it. Because they're all subdomains of the same root.

# Subdomains: prefixes attached to the root domain
clientsite.com          ← root / naked domain (the website)
www.clientsite.com      ← the classic "www" subdomain (often same as root)
blog.clientsite.com     ← a separate blog
api.clientsite.com      ← the API server
admin.clientsite.com    ← admin panel
mail.clientsite.com     ← email server

# A subdomain is just a DNS record that points to an IP or another domain
# You create subdomains in your DNS settings — no extra registration needed
# But they all depend on the root domain being registered and valid

# www vs. no-www:
# Both should work. Typically:
# - Set your "canonical" version (usually no-www or www, pick one)
# - Redirect the other to your canonical version with a 301
# - www.example.com → example.com (or vice versa)

# Wildcard subdomains:
# *.clientsite.com → catches any subdomain not explicitly defined
# Used by platforms like Vercel: your-app.vercel.app works for every customer
So every service they run under clientsite.com is offline right now — including their business email.

Yes. If they had used a separate domain for email, or a transactional email service like SendGrid, those would still be up. This is why large companies often register their email domain separately from their product domain.

Buy critical domains for 5–10 years upfront. Enable auto-renew. Set renewal alerts for 60 and 30 days before expiry. Keep the registrar account's email address one that will always exist and be monitored.

sections.title: Recovering the Domain — and Protecting It Next Time

blocks.v: 📍 The registrar confirms the domain can be recovered for a $200 redemption fee
Two hundred dollars to get back a domain we paid $12 for.

And we're lucky it's still in the redemption window. After this, a squatter would have it within hours of it going to auction. I've seen companies spend $5,000 buying back their own domain from squatters.

# The domain recovery plan:

# 1. Pay the redemption fee — domain restores within 24-72 hours
# 2. While waiting, set up a holding page on a new temp domain

# Once recovered — harden the account:

# Enable auto-renew immediately
Registrar settings → Auto-renew: ON

# Prepay for multiple years
# $12/year × 5 years = $60 now, never think about it until 2031

# Enable domain lock (Transfer Lock)
# Prevents unauthorized transfer to another registrar
# Turn off ONLY when you intentionally want to transfer

# Enable two-factor authentication on the registrar account
# The registrar account is the master key to your entire domain
# If someone hijacks the registrar account, they can redirect all DNS
# MFA on this account is not optional

# Set up monitoring — alert if domain stops resolving:
# UptimeRobot, Better Uptime, or Freshping (free tiers available)
# Alerts via email/SMS when site goes down
# Catches both server and DNS issues
Transfer lock — I've never heard of that.

Without transfer lock, anyone with access to your registrar account can move your domain to a different registrar in 48 hours. Domain hijacking is a real attack. Transfer lock forces any outbound transfer to go through a manual confirmation step. Always keep it on.

A domain is a lease, not a purchase — you rent from a registrar (Namecheap, Cloudflare, etc.) annually
Expiry stages: immediate loss of DNS → 30-day grace (normal price) → 30-day redemption ($150-300) → public auction
Subdomains (www, api, mail, blog) all depend on the root domain being valid — one expiry takes everything down
Must-do after buying any domain: enable auto-renew, enable transfer lock, enable 2FA on the registrar account
Prepay for 5-10 years on domains that are critical to your business
Set up uptime monitoring (UptimeRobot free tier) to alert you the moment DNS fails
WHOIS privacy hides your personal contact info from public lookup — enable it on registration
For beginners: Cloudflare Registrar offers domains at cost (no markup) and is also your DNS manager

title: Why Is the Site Showing "Not Secure"? (Episode 2)

blocks.v: 📍 Maya just launched a client's new website. One hour later, her phone rings.
The client says customers are emailing them asking if the site is hacked. They're seeing a warning that says the connection is "not secure."
What's the URL? http:// or https://?
http:// ... Is that bad?

It means the site has no SSL certificate. Every modern browser shows a "Not Secure" warning on HTTP sites — and Chrome started blocking form submissions on HTTP pages entirely. If the site has a login or a contact form, it's flagged.
I thought HTTPS was only for banks and shops.
That was true in 2010. Today, all websites are expected to use HTTPS. Google also penalises HTTP sites in search rankings. This needs to be fixed before the day is out.

Browsers have shown "Not Secure" warnings on HTTP pages since 2018. If a visitor sees this, the most common reaction is to leave immediately — not to investigate whether the content is actually dangerous.
📍 Sam explains what the padlock actually means

HTTPS uses TLS — Transport Layer Security. It does two things. First, it encrypts everything between the browser and the server, so nobody on the network can read the traffic. Second, it authenticates the server — the browser verifies that it's talking to the real site, not an impostor.

# What HTTP exposes to anyone on the same network:
# (coffee shop WiFi, your ISP, a compromised router)

HTTP request (visible to anyone sniffing traffic):
GET /login HTTP/1.1
Host: clientsite.com

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
username=maya@company.com&password=MyP@ssword123   ← PLAIN TEXT

# With HTTPS (TLS), the payload is encrypted:
# The network observer sees only:
# - That you connected to clientsite.com (hostname is visible in SNI)
# - The size and timing of requests
# - Nothing else — URL path, headers, body are all encrypted

# The certificate also prevents impersonation:
# If someone intercepts your traffic and serves a fake site,
# the browser checks: does this certificate match clientsite.com?
# Is it signed by a trusted Certificate Authority?
# If no: browser shows a hard error and blocks the page entirely
So on HTTP, the password goes over the network as readable text?

Yes. Anyone on the same network — same coffee shop WiFi, or an ISP that monitors traffic — can see every form submission, every cookie, every search. HTTPS encrypts all of that before it leaves the browser.

sections.title: Getting a Certificate with Let's Encrypt

blocks.v: 📍 Sam shows Maya how to get a free trusted SSL certificate in minutes

Before 2016, SSL certificates cost $50-$300 per year and took days to issue. Let's Encrypt changed all of that. Free, automated, and trusted by every major browser. It's now the standard for any non-commercial site.

# Install Certbot (the Let's Encrypt client) on Ubuntu:
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx

# Get and install a certificate for your domain (with Nginx):
sudo certbot --nginx -d clientsite.com -d www.clientsite.com
# Certbot will:
# 1. Verify you own the domain (checks a file on your server)
# 2. Generate a certificate signed by Let's Encrypt CA
# 3. Automatically update your Nginx config to use HTTPS
# 4. Schedule automatic renewal

# Certificate details after install:
# Valid for: 90 days
# Auto-renewal: Certbot renews at 60 days via a cron job
# You never need to manually renew

# Verify it worked:
curl -I https://clientsite.com
# HTTP/2 200
# Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000

# For cloud platforms / managed hosting — even easier:
# Vercel:    SSL is automatic on every deploy, no setup
# Netlify:   SSL is automatic on every deploy, no setup
# Cloudflare: enable 'Full (strict)' SSL in dashboard — done
# cPanel hosting: 'AutoSSL' in Lets Encrypt section — one click
Ninety days validity sounds short. Don't we have to keep renewing it?

Certbot handles it automatically. The short validity period is intentional — it limits the damage if a certificate is ever compromised, and forces automation. Most hosting panels and cloud platforms renew certificates without you ever noticing. It's the old 1-year certificates that people actually forgot to renew.

sections.title: Forcing HTTPS and Fixing Mixed Content

blocks.v: 📍 Certificate is installed. But some pages still show a warning.
The padlock is gone on some pages — it shows a triangle with an exclamation mark instead.
Mixed content. The page is served over HTTPS but it's loading some resources — images, stylesheets, scripts — over HTTP. The browser blocks them or downgrades the security indicator.
# Mixed content example (what the browser is seeing): https://clientsite.com/about ← HTTPS page (good) ↳ loads ← HTTP resource (bad) ↳ loads
HSTS means the browser remembers that this site is HTTPS-only and will refuse HTTP even if I accidentally type http://?

Exactly. And `includeSubDomains` means all your subdomains get the same protection automatically. Once HSTS is set, there's no way for an attacker to downgrade the connection — even if they intercept the first request.

After setting up HTTPS, check your site on **SSL Labs** (ssllabs.com/ssltest) — it gives an A/B/F grade and lists any weak cipher suites, expired intermediates, or misconfigured redirects. Aim for A or A+.

All websites need HTTPS in 2026 — browsers warn on HTTP, Google penalises it in rankings, and it blocks form submissions
HTTPS does two things: encrypts the connection (nobody on the network can read it) and authenticates the server (you're talking to the real site)
Let's Encrypt provides free, auto-renewing certificates — install via Certbot on Linux or enable in your hosting panel (Vercel/Netlify do it automatically)
Certificates expire every 90 days — but Certbot auto-renews at 60 days; you should never need to renew manually
Redirect all HTTP → HTTPS with a 301 redirect in your web server config
Mixed content: a page served over HTTPS must not load any resources over HTTP — find and fix with browser DevTools → Console
HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security header): tells browsers to use HTTPS for the next year, even without seeing your redirect
Check your setup at ssllabs.com — any score below A means something needs fixing

title: The DNS Change That Nobody Could See (Episode 3)

sections.title: The Migration That Worked on My Machine

blocks.v: 📍 Maya just finished migrating a website to a new, faster server.
Migration is done. I updated the A record to point to the new server IP. The site looks great on my end. New server, faster load times — everything is perfect.
When did you update the DNS?
About an hour ago.
The client just emailed. They're seeing the old site. Their customers are also seeing the old site. A few people on Twitter say the site won't load at all.
But it works for me! I'm literally looking at the new server right now.
DNS propagation. You made the change — but most of the internet hasn't heard about it yet.

DNS changes don't take effect instantly everywhere in the world. The update has to spread across thousands of caching servers globally — a process called DNS propagation that can take minutes or up to 48 hours, depending on one critical setting.
📍 Sam draws out the DNS lookup chain

When someone types your URL into a browser, their computer doesn't look up the IP address directly. It goes through a chain of servers, each of which might have a cached answer from the last time someone asked.

# DNS resolution chain (what happens when browser asks "where is clientsite.com?"):

1. Browser cache
   └─ Did I look this up recently? If yes and still valid → use it

2. Operating system cache / hosts file
   └─ Has the OS cached this? If yes and still valid → use it

3. Recursive resolver (your ISP or 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1)
   └─ The resolver your device is configured to use
   └─ It also has its own cache — checks it first

4. Root nameservers (13 clusters worldwide)
   └─ "I don't know clientsite.com, but .com is handled by Verisign"

5. TLD nameserver (Verisign for .com)
   └─ "clientsite.com is managed by ns1.namecheap.com"

6. Authoritative nameserver (your registrar or Cloudflare)
   └─ "clientsite.com A record = 203.0.113.42" ← the actual answer

# The resolver caches the answer from step 6
# and serves it to the next person who asks — without going all the way again
# How long it caches: controlled by the TTL value on the DNS record
So when I see the new site, it's because my resolver already picked up the updated record. But someone else's resolver is still serving the old cached answer.
Yes. And there are thousands of resolvers around the world, each with their own cache. Until each one's cache expires, they keep serving the old IP.

sections.title: TTL — The One Number That Controls Everything

blocks.v: 📍 Sam shows Maya the TTL on the old DNS records
TTL — Time To Live. It's a number, in seconds, attached to every DNS record. It tells resolvers: "cache this answer for this long before checking again." Your old A record had a TTL of 86400.

# TTL: Time To Live — how long resolvers cache the DNS answer
# Check current TTL on a record:
dig clientsite.com A
# ;; ANSWER SECTION:
# clientsite.com. 86400 IN A 198.51.100.1
#                 ^^^^^─── TTL in seconds = 24 hours

# After your DNS change:
# - Resolvers that cached BEFORE your change: still have the old IP for up to 24 hours
# - Resolvers that ask AFTER your change: immediately get the new IP
# - This is why some people see the new site and some see the old one — simultaneously

# The right approach for a planned migration:

# Step 1: 24-48 hours BEFORE migration
# Lower the TTL on your A record to 300 (5 minutes)
dig +short clientsite.com A  # confirm current IP, it's propagating at old TTL now
# Then change TTL from 86400 → 300 in your DNS panel
# Wait 24+ hours for the low-TTL to propagate everywhere

# Step 2: Do the migration
# Change the A record to the new server IP
# Now propagation takes at most 5 minutes, not 24 hours

# Step 3: After migration is confirmed stable
# Raise TTL back to 3600 (1 hour) or 86400 (24 hours)
# Lower TTL = more DNS queries = slightly more load on nameservers
Lower the TTL a day before, so when I actually make the change it propagates in 5 minutes instead of 24 hours. I should have done that first.
Every time. That's the migration checklist item zero — reduce TTL 24 hours before you touch the IP.

sections.title: The DNS Record Types You Actually Use

blocks.v: 📍 Maya notices several unfamiliar record types in the DNS panel and asks about them
There are all these other records in here — CNAME, MX, TXT, NS. What are they all for?
These are the ones you'll use for almost every site you ever set up.

# A record — most common: maps a hostname to an IPv4 address
clientsite.com     A      203.0.113.42       # root domain → server IP
www.clientsite.com A      203.0.113.42       # www → same server

# CNAME — maps a hostname to another hostname (not an IP)
# Used for services that give you a hostname instead of an IP
www.clientsite.com   CNAME  clientsite.com.        # www → root
blog.clientsite.com  CNAME  mysite.netlify.app.    # blog → Netlify
shop.clientsite.com  CNAME  mystore.myshopify.com. # shop → Shopify
# Rule: you cannot put a CNAME on the root domain (@) — use A or ALIAS instead

# MX record — mail routing: where to send email for @clientsite.com
clientsite.com  MX  10  aspmx.l.google.com.   # Google Workspace
clientsite.com  MX  20  alt1.aspmx.l.google.com.
# Lower priority number = tried first

# TXT record — plain text, used for verification and email authentication
clientsite.com  TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"  # SPF (anti-spam)
clientsite.com  TXT  "google-site-verification=abc123..."   # domain ownership proof

# NS record — which nameservers are authoritative for this domain
# Set by your registrar. If you use Cloudflare for DNS:
clientsite.com  NS  erin.ns.cloudflare.com.
clientsite.com  NS  ivan.ns.cloudflare.com.
So when I add my site to Google Workspace or Netlify and they say "add this TXT record to verify ownership," that's what the TXT record is for?

Exactly. The TXT record is a catch-all for anything that doesn't have its own dedicated record type. Domain verification, SPF and DKIM for email authentication, DMARC policies — all go in TXT records. You'll add TXT records constantly when wiring up new services.
Use **dnschecker.org** to see your DNS record from 25+ locations around the world simultaneously. It shows you exactly which regions have propagated and which are still serving the old record.

DNS maps human-readable domain names to IP addresses through a chain: browser → OS cache → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative nameserver
DNS propagation: changes don't take effect instantly — resolvers worldwide cache the old answer until their TTL expires
TTL (Time To Live): the number of seconds resolvers cache a DNS record. Default is often 86400 (24 hours).
Migration checklist: lower TTL to 300 (5 min) at least 24 hours before changing IPs — then propagation takes minutes, not days
Record types: A (hostname → IPv4), CNAME (hostname → hostname), MX (email routing), TXT (verification + SPF/DKIM), NS (which nameservers are authoritative)
CNAME cannot be placed on the root domain — use A record or an ALIAS/ANAME record instead
Check propagation with dnschecker.org — see which regions have your new record and which still show the old one
Most DNS providers (Cloudflare, Route 53) propagate globally in under 1 minute once you lower the TTL

title: We Launched on Shared Hosting and It Crashed (Episode 4)

blocks.v: 📍 Maya's side project just hit the front page of Product Hunt.
Sam! We're number three on Product Hunt! And — no. No no no. The site is returning a 500 error.
What are you hosted on?
Shared hosting. $4.99 a month plan. I got an email from them: "Your account has been suspended for excessive CPU usage. Please contact support."
How long ago did you launch?
Eleven minutes.

Classic. Shared hosting is built for low-traffic sites that run quietly in the background. The moment you get real traffic, you're using more than your "fair share" and they cut you off — automatically, instantly, with no warning.

**Shared hosting puts hundreds of websites on one server, sharing the same CPU and RAM.** When your site uses more than its thin slice, the host suspends your account to protect the other tenants. There is no auto-scaling, no burst capacity, and no grace period.
📍 Sam explains the hosting model that almost everyone starts on

Shared hosting is the apartment block of web hosting. One big building — one server. Hundreds of tenants — hundreds of websites. You share the elevator, the parking, the plumbing. It's cheap because everyone splits the cost.

# Shared hosting (the $4.99/month plan)
One physical server: 32 CPU cores, 128 GB RAM
Number of accounts on it: 400-1000 websites
Your guaranteed resources: none — you share everything
Your CPU limit: ~0.5-1% of total, enforced by throttling
Your RAM: ~64-256 MB before PHP processes are killed

# What happens when you get traffic:
# Normal day: 10 visitors/hour → 0.01% CPU → fine
# Product Hunt: 500 visitors/minute → 5% CPU → SUSPENDED

# What shared hosting is actually good for:
# - Static or near-static websites
# - Low-traffic personal sites or portfolios
# - WordPress blogs with < 1,000 visitors/day
# - Email hosting (often bundled)
# - Dev/staging environments
# - Hobby projects you won't launch publicly

# What it is NOT built for:
# - Anything with unpredictable traffic
# - Applications with a backend that does real work
# - Anything you care about staying online under load
So I've been building this on the wrong platform from the start.

Not the wrong platform for building — the wrong platform for launching. Shared hosting is fine for development and testing. The mistake was pointing a public launch at it without thinking about what would happen if it actually worked.
📍 Sam maps out the options from cheapest to most scalable
There's a clear progression of hosting options. Each step up gives you more control, more reliability, and more cost. The trick is picking the right rung for where your project actually is.

# The hosting ladder — cheapest to most scalable:

# 1. Static hosting — FREE
# Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages
# Hosts HTML/CSS/JS files — no server-side code
# CDN by default: your files are cached in 100+ locations worldwide
# Auto-scales to any traffic — Product Hunt, Hacker News, anything
# Free tier handles millions of page views
# Use when: your site has no backend, or your API is a separate service

# 2. Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) — $5-25/month
# Railway, Render, Fly.io, Heroku
# Deploy your Node/Python/Ruby app — they handle the server
# Auto-sleep on free tier, always-on from ~$5-7/month
# No server management: no SSH, no Nginx config, no patching
# Use when: you have a custom backend and want to focus on code, not ops

# 3. VPS (Virtual Private Server) — $5-20/month
# DigitalOcean Droplets, Linode (Akamai), Vultr, Hetzner
# Your own Linux VM with guaranteed CPU/RAM
# Full control: install anything, configure however you need
# You manage everything: security patches, Nginx, backups, SSL
# Use when: PaaS limits you or you need specific software control

# 4. Managed cloud — $20+/month, scales to any cost
# AWS, GCP, Azure
# Every service imaginable: compute, storage, databases, ML, CDN
# Auto-scaling, global, enterprise-grade SLA
# Steep learning curve and complex pricing
# Use when: you need to scale beyond what a single VPS can handle
My app has a Node.js backend. So PaaS like Railway is the right starting point — not VPS, not shared?

Yes. PaaS is the sweet spot for apps with a custom backend. You deploy with a git push, they handle the infrastructure. When you outgrow it — and you'll know when that is — the migration to a VPS or cloud is a deliberate choice, not a crisis.

sections.title: The Right Stack for Most Websites

blocks.v: 📍 Sam gives Maya a reusable framework for choosing hosting
Most websites fit into one of five patterns. Once you identify which pattern your site is, the hosting choice mostly makes itself.

# Pattern 1: Static marketing site / portfolio / docs
# Frontend: any static site generator (Next.js static export, Astro, Hugo)
# Hosting: Netlify or Vercel (free tier, CDN, auto-deploy from git)
# Cost: $0 for most sites
# Example: company homepage, blog, documentation site

# Pattern 2: WordPress or other CMS
# Hosting: managed WordPress (WP Engine, Kinsta) or DigitalOcean $6/mo VPS
# Managed WP: $25-50/month — handles caching, backups, updates
# DIY VPS: $6/month, but you configure and maintain everything yourself
# Example: content site, news site, simple business site

# Pattern 3: Custom backend app (Node, Python, Ruby, etc.)
# Hosting: Railway / Render / Fly.io (~$5-10/month to start)
# Database: included PostgreSQL (Railway) or separate managed DB ($5-15/month)
# Example: SaaS app, API, web app with user accounts

# Pattern 4: High-traffic or global audience
# Frontend: Vercel or Cloudflare Pages (still static)
# Backend: AWS/GCP/Azure with auto-scaling, or multiple VPS with load balancer
# Database: managed RDS/Cloud SQL or dedicated DB server
# Example: startup past product-market fit, 100k+ monthly visitors

# Pattern 5: E-commerce
# Small: Shopify ($29/month) — fastest, best ecosystem, no hosting to manage
# Custom: Pattern 3 + Stripe, or WooCommerce on managed WP
# Example: online store, subscription product
My project is Pattern 3 — custom Node backend. Railway it is. How fast can we get back online?

Railway can deploy from a GitHub repo in about three minutes. You write a Dockerfile or it detects Node automatically. Add environment variables in their dashboard, connect a managed Postgres, and you're live — on a platform that will actually handle the traffic.

Always test your site under load BEFORE a public launch. Tools like **k6** (k6.io, free) let you simulate hundreds of concurrent users in a terminal. If it can't handle 200 simultaneous users in a test, it will definitely buckle under a real launch.

Shared hosting puts hundreds of websites on one server — no guaranteed resources, no burst capacity. One traffic spike = account suspended.
Shared hosting is fine for: low-traffic sites, WordPress blogs under 1,000/day, dev environments, email hosting
Static hosting (Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare Pages): free, CDN by default, scales to unlimited traffic — best choice for any site with no backend
PaaS (Railway/Render/Fly.io): deploy custom backends with a git push — no server management, $5-10/month to start
VPS (DigitalOcean/Linode): your own guaranteed Linux VM — full control, but you manage everything yourself
Managed cloud (AWS/GCP): scales to anything, complex pricing, steep learning curve — use when VPS is not enough
For most custom apps: static frontend on Vercel/Netlify + PaaS backend + managed database covers 90% of use cases
Always load test before a public launch — k6 or Artillery can simulate hundreds of concurrent users for free
